title: Dental Implants in Markham: Complete Cost & Process Guide
seoTitle: Dental Implants Markham: Cost & Process Guide | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Full guide to dental implant costs and the step-by-step process in Markham. Reviewed by Dr. Neda Kadivar, D.D.S. Book a free consultation today.
excerpt: Thinking about dental implants in Markham? This guide covers every stage — from your first consultation and bone assessment to the final crown — along with transparent cost ranges and what Ontario insurance plans typically cover.
intro: Replacing a missing tooth with a dental implant is one of the most consequential decisions you can make for your long-term oral health. Unlike a bridge or removable denture, an implant replaces the entire tooth from root to crown, preserving the jawbone underneath and keeping neighbouring teeth exactly where they belong. At [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/dental-implants), Dr. Neda Kadivar has guided Markham patients through implant treatment for over 20 years, from single-tooth replacements to full-arch restorations.

This guide answers the questions patients bring to their first consultation: how much does the procedure cost in the Markham area, what happens at each appointment, how long does it take, and what should you watch out for? Read through each section before you book so you arrive with the right expectations — and the right questions.

sections.heading: What Is a Dental Implant?

blocks.text: A dental implant is a small titanium post that a dentist places surgically into the jawbone, where it serves as an artificial tooth root. Over the following weeks and months the bone grows around the post in a process called osseointegration, locking it permanently in place. Once the implant is stable, a connector piece called an abutment is attached to the top, and finally a custom-made porcelain crown is placed over it — creating a tooth that looks, feels and functions like the natural one it replaced.

The [Canadian Dental Association](https://www.cda-adc.ca/) recognises dental implants as the gold standard for tooth replacement, and clinical data consistently shows survival rates above 95 percent at ten years. That durability is why so many patients who initially explored dentures or bridges eventually choose implants instead — the investment pays off over a lifetime of use.

items: **Implant post** — titanium screw placed in the jawbone; designed to last a lifetime with proper care.
**Abutment** — connects the post to the crown; can be changed if the crown ever needs replacing.
**Crown** — the visible porcelain tooth; durable but may need replacement after 15–25 years of wear.
**Bone graft (sometimes)** — added when there is insufficient bone height or width to support the post.
**Sinus lift (sometimes)** — needed for upper back teeth where the sinus sits close to the jawbone.

sections.heading: The Step-by-Step Implant Process

blocks.text: Dental implant treatment is not a single appointment — it unfolds over several stages that allow the body to heal between steps. The total timeline from consultation to final crown varies from as little as three months for straightforward cases to a year or more when bone grafting is required first. Understanding each stage helps you plan your schedule and minimise surprises.

items: **Consultation and 3D imaging** — Dr. Kadivar evaluates your bone density, gum health and medical history using cone-beam CT scans to build a precise treatment plan.
**Bone grafting (if needed)** — performed at least three to six months before implant placement to build up areas with insufficient bone.
**Implant placement surgery** — a minor outpatient procedure under local anaesthesia, taking 60–90 minutes per implant.
**Osseointegration healing** — three to six months during which the titanium fuses with your jawbone; a temporary crown may be placed during this period.
**Abutment fitting and final crown** — once healed, the permanent crown is placed, completing your restoration.

blocks.text: Tip: Ask Dr. Kadivar about temporary crowns during the healing phase. Many patients can leave with a temporary tooth in place the same day as surgery, so they are never without a tooth in a visible position.

sections.heading: How Much Do Dental Implants Cost in Markham?

blocks.text: Implant costs in Markham typically range from **$3,000 to $6,000 per tooth** when the implant post, abutment and crown are bundled together — though complex cases with bone grafting or sinus lifts can push the total higher. The [Ontario Dental Association fee guide](https://www.oda.ca/) provides suggested fee ranges, and most Markham dental offices align their pricing reasonably close to those benchmarks.

It is important to compare quotes carefully. A low headline price that excludes the crown, abutment or 3D imaging can end up costing more than an all-inclusive quote. At our clinic we provide a written, itemised treatment plan before any work begins so you know exactly what each component costs. See our dedicated [implant cost page](/dental-implants/cost) for a full breakdown.

items: Single-tooth implant (post + abutment + crown): $3,000–$6,000.
Bone graft: $800–$2,500 depending on the volume of bone needed.
Sinus lift: $1,500–$3,000 per side.
Full-arch All-on-4 restoration: $20,000–$35,000 per arch.
Sedation (if desired): $300–$800 per appointment.

sections.heading: What Affects the Final Price?

blocks.text: Several clinical factors influence the total investment. The position of the missing tooth matters: back teeth endure more chewing force and occasionally require wider implants, while upper back teeth often need a sinus lift because the sinus cavity sits just above the bone. The number of teeth being replaced, the type of crown material (zirconia is more durable than standard porcelain-fused-to-metal), and whether sedation is requested all affect the final figure.

The dentist's experience and the imaging technology used also play a role. Cone-beam CT scans — which our clinic uses for every implant patient — cost more than standard x-rays but allow for far greater precision in planning and placement, reducing the risk of complications. Investing in a skilled, well-equipped practice from the start is almost always less expensive than correcting problems later.

sections.heading: Financing and Insurance Options in Ontario

blocks.text: Most private dental insurance plans in Ontario offer partial coverage for implants — commonly 50 percent of the surgical fee up to an annual maximum, though some plans exclude implants entirely. Review your policy's major restorative section, or ask our team to do a pre-determination for you before treatment begins. For those without insurance, the [Canadian Dental Care Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan.html) may cover a portion of implant-related costs for eligible households.

Our clinic offers in-office payment plans as well as third-party financing through dental finance providers, allowing patients to spread the cost over 12–60 months. Read the full breakdown of [dental implant insurance in Ontario](/blog/dental-implants-insurance-ontario) for details on what each plan typically covers and how to maximise your benefit.

sections.heading: Are You a Candidate for Dental Implants?

blocks.text: Most adults in good general health are suitable candidates, but a few factors need to be evaluated before proceeding. Adequate jawbone volume is essential — if significant bone loss has occurred since the tooth was lost, a [bone graft](/blog/bone-grafting-before-implants) may be required first. Controlled diabetes, well-managed gum disease and non-smokers generally achieve outcomes comparable to patients without those conditions, though healing may take longer.

Age is less of a barrier than many patients assume. Implants are appropriate for adults of any age, provided bone growth is complete (usually by the late teens). Even patients in their 70s and 80s regularly complete implant treatment with excellent results. The [same-day implant option](/blog/same-day-implants-candidate) is available for qualifying patients who have sufficient bone density and meet certain health criteria.

items: Sufficient jawbone density or willingness to proceed with grafting if needed.
Healthy gums — any active periodontal disease must be treated before implant surgery.
No uncontrolled systemic conditions such as unmanaged diabetes or active cancer treatment.
Non-smoker or willingness to quit during healing — smoking significantly raises failure risk.
Realistic expectations about the multi-stage timeline and recovery periods.

sections.heading: Recovery: What to Expect After Surgery

blocks.text: Most patients return to desk work within one to three days. Swelling and mild discomfort peak around day two or three and then improve steadily. Over-the-counter pain relievers such as ibuprofen and acetaminophen usually manage the discomfort well. A soft diet for the first week — think soup, scrambled eggs and yoghurt — protects the surgical site while it heals. Full details on the recovery timeline are in our article on [recovering from dental implant surgery](/blog/dental-implant-surgery-recovery).

Keeping the site clean is critical. Dr. Kadivar will provide a chlorhexidine mouth rinse and specific instructions for brushing around the implant. Smoking, alcohol and straw use are prohibited for at least a week after surgery to protect the blood clot that supports early healing. The implant itself is silent during osseointegration — patients often report they forget about it while waiting for the final crown.

sections.heading: Why Choose Smile Dental Arts Centre for Implants?

blocks.text: Dr. Neda Kadivar has placed and restored dental implants in Markham for over two decades and is a member of the [Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario](https://www.rcdso.org/) and the Ontario Dental Association. Every implant case begins with a 3D cone-beam CT scan for precise planning, and our clinic uses guided surgical stents for accurate placement. We speak English, Farsi and can accommodate patients who prefer Chinese-language care through a bilingual team member.

We are located at 3980 14th Ave, Unit 6, Markham — easily accessible from Unionville, Stouffville and Scarborough. Our clinic is open Monday through Friday with extended evening hours and every other Saturday, making it practical to schedule appointments around work. [Book a consultation](/appointments) and we will send you a written treatment plan, cost estimate and timeline within 48 hours.

title: Dental Implants vs. Dentures: Which Is Right for You?
seoTitle: Dental Implants vs. Dentures in Markham | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Comparing dental implants and dentures? This guide covers comfort, cost, longevity and bone health so Markham patients can choose the right tooth-replacement option.
excerpt: Implants and dentures both replace missing teeth, but they differ in comfort, cost, longevity and how they affect your jawbone. This guide walks through every comparison point so you can make a confident decision.
intro: If you are missing one tooth, several teeth or an entire arch, two options come up in almost every conversation: dental implants and dentures. Both restore your ability to chew and speak, and both can look natural — but that is roughly where the similarities end. The differences in long-term bone health, comfort and overall value are significant enough to be worth understanding before you commit to either path.

This article compares implants and dentures across the dimensions that matter most to patients: everyday comfort, cost upfront and over time, bone preservation, longevity and candidacy requirements. If you are still undecided after reading, [book a consultation](/appointments) and Dr. Kadivar will walk through your specific anatomy and budget to make a personalised recommendation.

sections.heading: Understanding the Fundamental Difference

blocks.text: A dental implant is anchored into the jawbone with a titanium post that functions exactly like a natural tooth root. Because it stimulates the bone every time you bite and chew, the bone stays healthy and dense over time. A denture, by contrast, sits on top of the gum tissue — either held in place by suction, dental adhesive or metal clasps on remaining teeth. The gum and bone beneath a denture receive no chewing stimulation, which causes the bone to gradually resorb (shrink) over the years.

This distinction matters more than most patients initially realise. Bone loss after tooth extraction is not just cosmetic — it changes the shape of your face, makes the denture fit looser over time, and limits your future implant options if you eventually want to switch. The [All-on-4 implant system](/dental-implants/all-on-4) and [implant-supported dentures](/dental-implants/implant-dentures) bridge the gap by anchoring a denture-like prosthetic to four or six implant posts, preserving bone while providing a full arch of teeth.

sections.heading: Comfort and Everyday Function

blocks.text: Implants feel and function like natural teeth. Patients report they forget the implant is there within a few months of receiving the final crown. There is no shifting when chewing steak or biting into an apple, no adhesive taste, and no need to remove anything at night. Speech is natural from the moment the crown is fitted because the implant does not move during talking.

Traditional full dentures require an adjustment period — sometimes several months — before patients feel confident chewing without slippage. Ill-fitting dentures cause sore spots on the gums that require multiple adjustment appointments. Even well-fitting dentures typically allow only about 20–25 percent of normal chewing force, compared to near-100 percent with implants. Partial dentures that clip onto remaining teeth can loosen those anchor teeth over time, potentially causing additional tooth loss.

items: **Implants:** chew with full force, no slippage, no adhesive, no removal required.
**Dentures:** 20–25% chewing efficiency initially, may slip, require adhesive for some patients.
**Implant-supported dentures:** clip onto 2–4 implants for dramatically improved stability over conventional dentures.
**Partial dentures:** can loosen adjacent teeth via the metal clasps used to hold them in place.
**Social confidence:** implant patients report higher confidence in social and professional settings in long-term studies.

sections.heading: Cost Comparison: Now vs. Over Time

blocks.text: The upfront cost of a full set of conventional dentures ranges from roughly $1,500 to $4,000 per arch, significantly less than the $20,000–$35,000 investment for an [All-on-4 implant restoration](/blog/all-on-4-implants-markham). However, dentures typically need relining every two to four years as the gum and bone change shape, and replacing them every seven to ten years as wear accumulates. Over a 20-year period the total cost of ownership for a denture can approach or exceed the cost of a well-placed implant restoration.

For single tooth replacement, the comparison is even clearer. A traditional [dental bridge](/blog/dental-bridge-vs-implant) costs $2,000–$4,000 but typically lasts 10–15 years and requires grinding down the two healthy teeth on either side. A single implant at $3,000–$6,000 requires no alteration to neighbouring teeth, and the implant post itself is designed to last a lifetime. Many patients find the long-term maths strongly favour the implant.

sections.heading: Bone Health: The Hidden Advantage of Implants

blocks.text: Within the first year after a tooth is lost, the jawbone at that site loses approximately 25 percent of its width. The resorption continues more slowly over subsequent years but never stops as long as the bone lacks stimulation. This is why patients who wore full dentures for many years often show a dramatically sunken lower face — the bone that used to support their teeth has largely disappeared.

Implants are the only tooth-replacement option that halts this process by delivering chewing forces directly into the bone. This has consequences beyond appearance: patients with significant bone loss who eventually want implants may require extensive — and expensive — bone grafting. Placing implants sooner rather than later often avoids that need. Read [what happens if you wait too long to replace a missing tooth](/blog/waiting-to-replace-missing-tooth) for a full explanation of the bone-loss timeline.

sections.heading: Longevity: How Long Does Each Option Last?

blocks.text: Implant posts, once osseointegrated, have a projected lifespan of 25 years or more — many studies document survival rates above 90 percent at 20 years. The crown on top may eventually chip or wear and require replacement, typically after 15–25 years depending on materials and habits. Conventional full dentures, by contrast, need relining every two to four years and full replacement approximately every seven to ten years.

The longevity advantage of implants compounds over time. A patient who receives an implant at age 45 may need the crown replaced once in their lifetime and never need to reline or refit the implant structure itself. The same patient with a full denture will spend considerable time and money on relines, repairs and replacements over the ensuing decades.

items: Implant post: designed for lifetime function, 25+ year documented survival rates.
Implant crown: typically 15–25 years before replacement.
Full conventional denture: replacement every 7–10 years, relining every 2–4 years.
Implant-supported overdenture: the denture portion replaced every 5–8 years; the implants last a lifetime.
Partial denture: variable, typically 5–10 years; clasps may loosen adjacent teeth.

sections.heading: Candidacy: Who Can Get Each Option?

blocks.text: Dentures can be fitted to almost any patient regardless of bone density, making them a practical choice when health conditions, financial constraints or timeline limitations rule out implants. Implants require adequate bone volume, controlled systemic health and, ideally, non-smoking status. Patients with osteoporosis, active cancer treatment or very low bone density may not qualify for standard implants but may be candidates for [bone grafting](/blog/bone-grafting-before-implants) as a prerequisite.

Age is not a disqualifier for implants. The [Canadian Dental Association](https://www.cda-adc.ca/) notes that implant success rates in older adults are comparable to younger populations, provided bone density is adequate and systemic conditions are managed. A 3D cone-beam CT scan during your consultation with Dr. Kadivar will determine precisely how much bone is available and what — if any — preparatory procedures are needed.

sections.heading: Making the Right Choice for Your Situation

blocks.text: There is no universally correct answer — the right choice depends on your bone density, overall health, budget, timeline and personal priorities. Some patients choose dentures initially and transition to [implant-supported dentures](/dental-implants/implant-dentures) later once finances allow. Others find that the upfront investment in implants aligns better with their long-term goals and lifestyle. The key is making the decision with accurate information rather than assumptions.

At Smile Dental Arts Centre, we offer a thorough consultation that includes 3D imaging, a detailed cost comparison for each option relevant to your case, and honest guidance on which approach will serve you best over the long term. [Book your consultation](/appointments) to get a personalised comparison — not just a generic brochure.

Did you know? Implant-supported dentures combine the stability of implants with the affordability of a prosthetic arch, making them an excellent middle ground for patients replacing a full arch of teeth. Four implants can anchor an entire upper or lower set of teeth permanently or as a snap-in overdenture.

title: How Long Do Dental Implants Last?
seoTitle: How Long Do Dental Implants Last? | Markham Implant Guide
metaDescription: Dental implants are designed to last a lifetime — but what does the evidence say? Learn what affects implant longevity and how to protect your investment.
primaryKeyword: how long do dental implants last
excerpt: With proper care, the titanium implant post is designed to last a lifetime. This article explains what clinical evidence says about long-term survival rates, what factors most influence longevity, and what you can do to protect your investment.
intro: One of the most common questions patients ask during a dental implant consultation is: how long will this actually last? It is a fair question — implants represent a significant investment, and the answer shapes whether they make financial sense compared to other tooth-replacement options. The short answer is that a well-placed implant from a skilled dentist, with proper home care, is designed to last the rest of your life.

That said, there are important nuances. The implant post that integrates with your bone is the most durable component; the crown sitting on top is subject to ordinary wear and may need replacement after 15–25 years. This article walks through the clinical evidence, the factors that most influence how long an implant lasts, and the daily habits that protect your investment for decades to come.

sections.heading: What the Clinical Evidence Shows

blocks.text: Long-term clinical studies consistently show implant survival rates above 90 percent at 10 years and above 85 percent at 20 years. Some studies tracking patients for 25–30 years report survival rates approaching 95 percent when implants were placed by experienced practitioners in healthy bone. The [Canadian Dental Association](https://www.cda-adc.ca/) recognises dental implants as the most durable tooth-replacement option available today.

It is important to distinguish between implant survival (the post remaining in place and functional) and implant success (the post functioning without any complications). Success rates are somewhat lower than survival rates because they include minor issues like peri-implant bone maintenance. However, even by the stricter success definition, implants outperform bridges and dentures in almost every long-term comparison.

sections.heading: The Three-Part Lifespan: Post, Abutment and Crown

blocks.text: A dental implant has three components, and each has a different expected lifespan. The **titanium post** is designed to last your entire life once osseointegration is complete — provided you maintain good oral hygiene and do not develop peri-implantitis (infection around the implant). The **abutment** that connects post to crown also typically lasts decades; it may occasionally need tightening or replacement if the screw loosens.

The **crown** is the component most likely to need attention over time. Porcelain crowns are durable but do chip and wear under the forces of daily chewing. Most implant crowns last 15–25 years before needing replacement — good news being that replacing a crown is a relatively minor procedure; the implant post underneath stays exactly where it is. Choosing a harder material like **zirconia** for the crown can extend its lifespan significantly.

items: **Titanium post:** lifetime — once integrated with bone, designed to stay permanently.
**Abutment:** 20+ years in most cases; screw may need periodic tightening.
**Standard porcelain-fused-to-metal crown:** 15–20 years with good care.
**Zirconia crown:** potentially 20–30 years due to superior hardness and chip resistance.
**Full-arch prosthesis (All-on-4):** the prosthetic teeth need replacement every 10–20 years; the implant posts last a lifetime.

sections.heading: Factors That Shorten Implant Lifespan

blocks.text: The single biggest risk factor for implant failure is **peri-implantitis** — a bacterial infection of the tissue and bone surrounding the implant, similar to gum disease around natural teeth. It typically develops from inadequate brushing and flossing around the implant site. Left untreated, peri-implantitis causes progressive bone loss that can eventually loosen the implant. Early detection during routine check-ups is critical, which is why we recommend professional cleanings every three to six months for implant patients.

**Smoking** is the second most influential risk factor. Smokers have significantly higher implant failure rates than non-smokers — some studies show three to four times the risk. Nicotine restricts blood flow to healing tissue, slowing osseointegration and reducing the immune response to bacteria. If you smoke, Dr. Kadivar will discuss cessation support and what it means for your specific treatment plan. [Uncontrolled diabetes](/blog/dental-implants-markham-cost-process), bruxism (teeth grinding) and poor bone density also increase risk.

items: Smoking and tobacco use — significantly impairs healing and raises infection risk.
Uncontrolled diabetes — slows healing; well-managed diabetes is not a contraindication.
Bruxism (teeth grinding) — excessive clenching forces can fracture the crown and loosen the abutment.
Inadequate oral hygiene — allows biofilm to accumulate around the implant and cause peri-implantitis.
Poor bone quality at placement — low-density bone integrates less reliably and may require grafting first.

sections.heading: Daily Habits That Protect Your Implant

blocks.text: Caring for an implant is very similar to caring for a natural tooth. Brush twice a day with a soft-bristled brush and use an interdental brush or floss threader to clean under the crown where it meets the gum — this is the area most prone to biofilm accumulation. An electric toothbrush is a helpful upgrade for implant patients because it removes more plaque per stroke than a manual brush.

Avoid chewing ice, hard candies or fingernails, which apply sudden extreme forces that can chip the crown. If you clench or grind at night, ask Dr. Kadivar about a custom night guard — this single appliance can dramatically extend the life of both your crown and the abutment screw beneath it. See our [recovering from dental implant surgery](/blog/dental-implant-surgery-recovery) article for detailed care instructions during the healing phase.

Best practice: Treat the tissue around your implant exactly as you would treat healthy gum around a natural tooth. Floss daily, use an antibacterial rinse if your dentist recommends it, and attend every recall appointment — even if the implant feels perfect.

sections.heading: The Role of Routine Check-ups and Professional Cleaning

blocks.text: Even patients who are diligent at home benefit from professional cleaning around implant sites. Dental hygienists use instruments specifically designed for titanium surfaces — standard metal scalers can scratch the post surface and create microscopic harbours for bacteria. Plastic or resin-tipped instruments and ultrasonic scalers with non-metal tips are the tools of choice. At our Markham clinic, hygienists trained in implant maintenance perform all recall cleanings.

During your annual check-up, Dr. Kadivar checks the implant for mobility, inspects the crown for chips, probes the peri-implant tissue to detect early signs of inflammation, and takes a periapical x-ray to monitor bone levels. Catching and treating early peri-implant mucositis (reversible gum inflammation) before it advances to bone-destructive peri-implantitis is the most important thing a check-up can accomplish.

sections.heading: What Happens If an Implant Fails?

blocks.text: Early failure (within the first few months) is rare — occurring in 1–2 percent of cases in healthy patients — and is usually related to the osseointegration process not completing as expected. The implant may feel mobile or cause persistent pain. In these cases the implant is removed, the site is allowed to heal, and after a few months a replacement implant is placed. Most patients who re-implant after an early failure achieve successful integration the second time.

Late failure (years after successful integration) almost always involves peri-implantitis that was not caught or treated in time. The good news is that with vigilant maintenance the likelihood of late failure is very low. Knowing the warning signs — bleeding or pus around the implant, visible bone loss on x-ray, or a slightly mobile crown — lets you seek treatment early before the implant is at risk.

sections.heading: Is a Dental Implant Worth the Investment?

blocks.text: When you factor in the 25+ year lifespan of the implant post, the avoidance of bone loss, the preservation of adjacent natural teeth, and the near-natural function and aesthetics, dental implants consistently show strong cost-effectiveness over a lifetime compared to dentures or bridges that need periodic repair and replacement. The [dental implant cost guide](/dental-implants/cost) at our clinic has a side-by-side 20-year cost comparison.

Dr. Neda Kadivar has helped hundreds of Markham patients replace missing teeth with implants that are still functioning perfectly a decade or more later. If you are ready to learn whether an implant is right for your specific situation — including your bone anatomy, medical history and budget — [book a consultation](/appointments) at Smile Dental Arts Centre today.

title: Are Dental Implants Covered by Insurance in Ontario?
seoTitle: Dental Implants Insurance Ontario | What Is Covered? | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Wondering if dental implants are covered by insurance in Ontario? Learn what private plans typically pay, how the CDCP applies, and financing options available in Markham.
excerpt: Coverage for dental implants in Ontario varies widely by plan. This guide explains what private insurance typically pays, how the federal Canadian Dental Care Plan may help, and what financing options are available when coverage falls short.
intro: One of the first questions Markham patients ask after hearing the cost of dental implants is whether their insurance will cover any of it. The honest answer is: it depends on your plan, and possibly — but often only partially. Understanding exactly how dental insurance handles implants, what you can realistically expect from public programs, and how to maximise whatever benefit you do have will save you both money and frustration.

This article breaks down coverage under typical Ontario employer plans, explains the federal [Canadian Dental Care Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan.html) and its implications for implants, and outlines the financing options our Markham clinic offers to patients whose coverage falls short of the full treatment cost.

sections.heading: How Private Dental Insurance Handles Implants

blocks.text: Private dental insurance plans in Ontario typically divide coverage into three categories: basic (cleanings, fillings, x-rays), basic-major (root canals, extractions) and major restorative (crowns, bridges, dentures, implants). Implants almost always fall under major restorative, which is where most plans apply their lowest reimbursement percentage — commonly 50 percent — and their annual or lifetime maximums.

However, many older employer plans were written before implants became commonplace and exclude them by name, covering only the crown portion as a prosthetic tooth while excluding the surgical placement of the implant post. Read your policy under the major restorative section carefully, or call your insurer before booking treatment to ask specifically: does this plan cover the surgical placement of a dental implant and the abutment, or only the crown?

items: **50% coverage of eligible fees** is the most common implant benefit in Ontario group plans.
**Annual maximums** of $1,000–$2,500 per year apply — and implant treatment may exhaust your entire annual benefit in one procedure.
**Lifetime maximums** on implants specifically appear in some plans, capping total implant reimbursement at $1,500–$3,000 per tooth.
**Waiting periods** of 12–24 months may apply for major restorative work if your plan is new.
**Pre-determination** — always submit a pre-determination form before starting treatment so you know exactly what your insurer will pay.

sections.heading: The Canadian Dental Care Plan (CDCP) and Implants

blocks.text: The federal [Canadian Dental Care Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan.html) launched in 2024 to provide dental coverage for households with an adjusted net family income below $90,000 that do not have access to private dental insurance. The CDCP covers a range of services based on the federal fee schedule, and coverage for certain prosthetic services — including implant-related work — is included, though the specific fees paid and eligibility criteria evolve as the program matures.

Patients who qualify for the CDCP and are considering [dental implants in Markham](/dental-implants) should bring their CDCP benefit card to their consultation. Our clinic is enrolled to bill the CDCP directly, and we will perform a benefit check before recommending a treatment plan so you know upfront what the program will pay toward implant surgery, bone grafting and the final crown.

sections.heading: Splitting Treatment Across Plan Years to Maximise Benefits

blocks.text: Because dental implant treatment naturally unfolds in stages — consultation and imaging, then implant placement surgery, then the final crown — it is often possible to schedule procedures across two calendar years to take advantage of annual maximums twice. For example: implant placement surgery in November or December of one year, then the abutment and crown placement in January or February of the following year. Each claim draws on a separate annual maximum.

Our treatment coordinator at Smile Dental Arts Centre is experienced in helping patients time their appointments to align with insurance renewal dates. This is entirely legitimate — you are simply scheduling clinically appropriate stages of treatment when they happen to coincide with plan year boundaries. Patients who plan this way can recover an additional $1,000–$2,500 in benefits compared to those who rush through treatment in a single year.

sections.heading: Financing Options When Coverage Falls Short

blocks.text: Even with insurance, most patients have an out-of-pocket balance after implant treatment. Our clinic addresses this in two ways: in-house payment plans that allow you to pay the balance in monthly installments with no interest for up to 12 months, and referrals to dental financing companies that offer extended terms of 24–60 months. Monthly payments on a single-tooth implant at these terms are often comparable to what a patient would spend on coffee or a gym membership.

Some patients also explore their RRSP or TFSA, or use a health spending account (HSA) from a self-directed employer plan, to pay for dental implants with pre-tax or already-sheltered funds. The [Ontario Dental Association](https://www.oda.ca/) recommends patients review all available benefit structures before assuming they will carry the entire cost out of pocket.

items: In-house payment plans: spread treatment cost over 6–12 months with no interest.
Third-party dental financing: terms from 24 to 60 months; interest rates vary by provider.
Health spending accounts (HSA): employer-provided HSAs are often forgotten sources of dental funds.
CDCP pre-determination: always check your CDCP benefit before treatment to know exact coverage.
Split billing across calendar years: maximise two annual maximums for multi-stage implant treatment.

sections.heading: What the Pre-Determination Process Looks Like

blocks.text: A pre-determination (sometimes called prior authorisation) is a request your dental office sends to your insurer describing the planned treatment using standardised codes. The insurer responds — usually within 10–14 business days — with an estimate of what it will pay based on your current benefit year balance, your plan limits and the fee schedule it uses. This is an estimate, not a guarantee, but it is close enough to plan around.

Our treatment coordinators submit pre-determinations on behalf of every implant patient before scheduling surgery. If the response reveals your plan does not cover implants at all, we will discuss alternative treatment plans or financing. If it confirms coverage, we factor the insurer payment into your treatment cost estimate so you see exactly what remains. There are no surprises in our billing process.

sections.heading: Tax Deductions for Dental Work in Canada

blocks.text: Eligible dental expenses not reimbursed by insurance qualify as medical expenses for the federal Medical Expense Tax Credit (METC). For the 2025 tax year, the METC allows you to claim qualifying medical expenses exceeding the lesser of 3 percent of your net income or $2,635. Dental implant costs — including the surgery, bone grafting and crown — are all eligible. Keep all receipts and submit them with your T1 return in the spring following treatment.

The tax credit does not eliminate the cost, but for a patient in the 26 percent marginal bracket who spent $5,000 on implants, the credit could return $600–$800 in tax savings. Patients with large medical expense years — such as when several family members have significant treatments — often find the METC particularly valuable. Consult a tax professional to optimise your claim.

sections.heading: Getting Started at Our Markham Clinic

blocks.text: At [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/dental-implants), we handle the insurance paperwork so you do not have to. From submitting your pre-determination to directly billing your insurer on the day of treatment, our administrative team manages every step. We also provide a written estimate that shows the full treatment cost, your expected insurance contribution and your balance — clearly, before you make any decisions.

Ready to understand exactly what your plan covers for dental implants in Markham? [Book a consultation](/appointments) with Dr. Neda Kadivar. We will review your current benefit card, run a benefit check, and give you a transparent financial picture of your options before any treatment begins.

Pro tip: Bring every dental insurance card you hold — including your spouse or partner's plan — to your consultation. Coordinating benefits between two plans (called dual coverage) can sometimes eliminate or dramatically reduce your out-of-pocket cost for implant treatment.

title: All-on-4 Implants: What Markham Patients Should Know
seoTitle: All-on-4 Dental Implants Markham | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: All-on-4 implants replace a full arch of teeth with just four implants. Learn how the procedure works, what it costs in Markham, and whether you are a candidate.
excerpt: All-on-4 dental implants replace an entire arch of missing or failing teeth with a fixed, non-removable prosthesis supported by just four strategically angled implant posts. This guide covers how it works, candidacy, cost and recovery.
intro: Losing most or all of your teeth — whether from gum disease, decay or injury — is a life-changing event. Conventional full dentures are one solution, but many patients find the slippage, reduced chewing ability and ongoing maintenance frustrating. The All-on-4 system offers a fundamentally different approach: four titanium implants are placed at precise angles in the jaw, and a fixed full-arch prosthesis is attached — often on the same day as surgery.

All-on-4 has become one of the most requested implant procedures at [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/dental-implants/all-on-4) in Markham. This guide explains exactly how the procedure works, who qualifies, what the recovery involves and what patients can expect to pay in the Markham area.

sections.heading: How the All-on-4 Concept Works

blocks.text: The All-on-4 concept was designed to maximise bone use while minimising the number of implants needed to support a full arch of teeth. Two implants are placed vertically at the front of the jaw where bone is typically most abundant, and two implants are placed at 45-degree angles toward the back — allowing them to engage more bone and avoid the sinus cavities in the upper jaw. This angled placement is the key innovation: it makes All-on-4 feasible for many patients who lack sufficient bone for standard rear implants.

A temporary full-arch prosthesis is typically attached on the day of surgery, meaning patients leave the clinic with a complete, fixed set of teeth. After a healing period of three to six months — during which osseointegration takes place — the temporary prosthesis is replaced with a final zirconia or acrylic-on-titanium prosthesis designed for long-term use. Compare this to [conventional implant-supported dentures](/dental-implants/implant-dentures), which snap on and off, or traditional dentures, which have no implant support at all.

sections.heading: All-on-4 vs. Traditional Dentures

blocks.text: Traditional dentures rest on the gums and rely on suction or adhesive for stability. They allow roughly 20–25 percent of natural chewing force and require removal for daily cleaning. Because there are no implants stimulating the bone, the jaw continues to resorb over time, causing the denture to fit progressively less well and changing the shape of the face. All-on-4 implants halt this bone loss and provide chewing forces approaching those of natural teeth.

Patients who switch from conventional dentures to All-on-4 almost universally report a dramatic improvement in confidence, comfort and dietary range. Foods that were off-limits with a denture — crunchy vegetables, tough meats, whole apples — become possible again. The fixed nature of the prosthesis also eliminates the social anxiety many denture wearers experience about their teeth shifting in public.

items: All-on-4 provides 70–90% of natural chewing force vs. 20–25% with conventional dentures.
Fixed, non-removable: no adhesives, no removal at night, no slippage when speaking.
Bone preservation: implants stimulate the jaw and prevent the ongoing resorption that dentures allow.
Cleaning: brush in place like natural teeth; no soaking solutions required.
Facial structure: preventing bone loss preserves the natural contour of cheeks and chin.

sections.heading: The All-on-4 Procedure: Step by Step

blocks.text: Treatment begins with a cone-beam CT scan to create a 3D model of the jaw. Using this model, Dr. Kadivar plans the exact position and angle of each of the four implants digitally before surgery begins. On procedure day, any remaining teeth are extracted (if needed), the four implants are placed, and a temporary full-arch prosthesis is screwed onto the implants — all in a single surgical session typically lasting three to four hours.

The patient recovers on the temporary prosthesis for three to six months while osseointegration takes place. Follow-up appointments check healing and adjust the temporary bite as needed. Once implants are confirmed fully integrated by x-ray, impressions are taken for the final, custom-made prosthesis. The final prosthesis is installed at a subsequent appointment and checked for fit, aesthetics and occlusion.

sections.heading: Who Is a Candidate for All-on-4?

blocks.text: All-on-4 was specifically engineered for patients who have lost most or all of their teeth and have experienced some degree of bone loss. The angled posterior implants allow the system to work in bone volumes that would not support standard implants placed vertically — which is why many patients who were told they needed extensive bone grafting for conventional implants are suitable for All-on-4 without grafting.

Patients should be in reasonably good general health, free of uncontrolled systemic conditions, and ideally non-smoking or willing to quit for the duration of healing. A 3D scan at consultation will show whether the anterior bone — where the front two implants sit — is sufficient. The vast majority of patients who present with most or all teeth missing qualify for All-on-4, often without additional bone grafting.

All-on-4 works for both the upper and lower arch, and some patients have both done simultaneously. Upper jaw placement is slightly more complex due to the proximity of the sinus cavity, but angled implant placement usually bypasses the sinus without a sinus lift procedure.

sections.heading: Cost of All-on-4 in Markham

blocks.text: All-on-4 treatment in the Markham area typically ranges from **$20,000 to $35,000 per arch**. This range reflects the complexity of individual cases, whether extractions are included, the material chosen for the final prosthesis (acrylic-on-titanium is less expensive than full-zirconia), and the type of sedation used. Full-arch treatment for both upper and lower jaws falls in the $35,000–$60,000 range depending on complexity.

While these figures are higher than the cost of conventional dentures, the all-inclusive nature of All-on-4 (fixed teeth, no ongoing adhesive costs, no relining every few years) means the long-term cost comparison is often more favourable for implants than it first appears. Our clinic offers financing with monthly payment plans, and some patients coordinate benefits across two plan years to maximise insurance coverage. See our [dental implants cost guide](/dental-implants/cost) for a detailed breakdown.

sections.heading: Recovery After All-on-4 Surgery

blocks.text: All-on-4 surgery is more extensive than single-tooth implant surgery, and recovery reflects that. Most patients take three to five days away from work and social activities. Swelling is notable for the first week and peaks around day two or three. A prescription or strong over-the-counter pain reliever manages discomfort, and a soft diet — soups, smoothies, yoghurt and soft cooked foods — is maintained for four to eight weeks to protect healing bone.

Patients leave with a fully functional set of temporary teeth, which means they can speak and eat (carefully) from day one. The temporary prosthesis is not designed for full chewing force — treating it gently is essential. By month three or four, most patients feel entirely back to normal. The full recovery timeline and care instructions are available in our [dental implant surgery recovery guide](/blog/dental-implant-surgery-recovery).

sections.heading: Finding the Right Markham Dentist for All-on-4

blocks.text: All-on-4 requires a dentist with specific training in guided implant surgery and full-arch prosthetics. It is not a procedure offered by all general dentists, and outcomes are closely tied to the precision of implant planning and placement. Ask potential providers whether they use 3D cone-beam CT imaging, digital surgical guides, and whether the final prosthesis is fabricated in a certified dental laboratory. At our clinic, every All-on-4 case is planned digitally and executed with guided stents for millimetre-level precision.

Dr. Neda Kadivar is a member of the [Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario](https://www.rcdso.org/) and has provided full-arch implant restorations to Markham patients for over two decades. [Book a consultation](/appointments) to receive a complete 3D treatment plan, cost estimate and timeline — with no obligation to proceed.

title: Recovering from Dental Implant Surgery: Timeline & Tips
seoTitle: Dental Implant Surgery Recovery: Timeline & Tips | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: What to expect after dental implant surgery in Markham: a week-by-week recovery timeline, diet tips, pain management and warning signs. Reviewed by Dr. Neda Kadivar.
excerpt: Recovery from dental implant surgery is usually milder than patients expect. This guide walks through the week-by-week timeline, explains what is normal versus concerning, covers diet and pain management, and gives you the best practices for protecting your implant during healing.
intro: The anxiety most patients feel before dental implant surgery is often far greater than the experience warrants. For the majority of single-tooth implant placements, discomfort is manageable with over-the-counter pain relievers, swelling peaks and subsides within a week, and most people return to desk work within a day or two. Understanding exactly what to expect — and what signals to watch for — helps you recover with confidence rather than uncertainty.

This recovery guide is written for patients at [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/dental-implants/procedure) in Markham who have had, or are about to have, a dental implant placed. It covers the first 24 hours, the first week, the osseointegration period, and the long-term habits that protect the implant for decades.

sections.heading: The First 24 Hours After Surgery

blocks.text: Immediately after surgery you will feel numb from the local anaesthetic — this typically lasts two to four hours. Do not eat hot food or test the surgical area with your tongue or fingers during this time, as you cannot feel what you are doing accurately. Bite gently on the gauze pad provided by Dr. Kadivar for the first hour to control any oozing; light pink-tinged saliva for several hours is entirely normal, but bright red bleeding should be reported.

Take your first dose of prescribed pain reliever or ibuprofen before the anaesthetic wears off — this is the most effective way to stay ahead of discomfort. Apply an ice pack to the outside of your face in 20-minutes-on, 20-minutes-off cycles for the first six hours to minimise swelling. Sleep with your head slightly elevated that night to reduce fluid pooling in the surgical site.

items: Do not smoke, use a straw or spit forcefully — this can dislodge the blood clot.
Eat only cool, soft foods: yoghurt, smoothies, mashed potato, scrambled eggs.
Take prescribed antibiotics exactly as directed to prevent infection.
Apply ice packs for the first six hours to minimise swelling.
Rest — physical exertion raises blood pressure and can increase bleeding.

sections.heading: Days 2–7: The Peak and Decline of Swelling

blocks.text: Swelling typically worsens over the first two to three days before improving. This is normal and is not a sign of infection on its own. By day three or four most patients notice a clear turning point — the swelling begins to recede and discomfort diminishes. Bruising on the cheek or neck area is also normal and will fade over one to two weeks. Switch from ice packs to warm compresses after 48 hours to help bruising resolve faster.

Continue the soft diet through the first week. Avoid anything that requires biting down hard or that could dislodge the forming blood clot around the implant. Warm salt-water rinses — half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water, gently swished — can begin on day two and should be done after every meal to keep the area clean without disturbing healing tissue.

Warning: Contact Dr. Kadivar promptly if you experience increasing pain after day three (pain should be decreasing, not increasing), a fever above 38°C, pus or foul taste around the implant site, or an implant that feels loose or mobile.

sections.heading: Weeks 2–4: Returning to Normal

blocks.text: By the end of the second week most patients have returned to their full regular diet, resumed exercise and are managing without any pain medication. The gum tissue around the implant will look more normal, though some mild pinkness may persist. You can brush directly around the implant site with a soft toothbrush — gently at first, then with normal pressure as comfort allows.

Flossing around the implant is important during this phase. Use a floss threader or dental implant floss designed to slide under the gum line without catching. An antibacterial mouth rinse recommended by Dr. Kadivar can supplement brushing, particularly in the first few weeks. Avoid whitening products around the implant site — they do not affect the titanium or crown material and can irritate healing tissue.

sections.heading: The Osseointegration Phase: Months 1–6

blocks.text: Osseointegration — the process by which the jawbone grows around and fuses to the titanium implant post — takes three to six months for most patients, and up to twelve months for those who had bone grafting first. During this phase you will not feel much of anything at the implant site; it becomes silent as the bone quietly does its work. However, this is the most critical period for the implant's long-term success.

Avoid habits that apply unexpected forces to the implant during osseointegration: chewing ice, very hard candies, or using the temporary crown as a bottle opener. If you have a night-grinding habit, ask about a temporary night guard — protecting the implant during sleep is particularly important during the integration phase. The [same-day implants](/dental-implants/same-day) protocol uses immediate-load implants that allow earlier crown placement, but they still require careful diet management during healing.

sections.heading: Diet During Recovery: What to Eat (and Avoid)

blocks.text: A soft diet is not a punishment — many patients discover it is a good opportunity to explore nutritious soups, smoothies and well-cooked vegetables. The key principle is avoiding anything that requires biting down with significant force in the implant area, anything very hard or crunchy, and anything very hot (which can dilate blood vessels and increase bleeding). Cold foods like yoghurt and cold smoothies are particularly soothing in the first 48 hours.

items: Week 1 — ideal: smoothies, yoghurt, soft scrambled eggs, soup, mashed vegetables, soft fish.
Week 1 — avoid: hard bread, crunchy snacks, chewy meat, very hot drinks and soups.
Weeks 2–4: gradually reintroduce most foods; continue to avoid chewing directly on the implant side.
After crown placement: treat the crown like a natural tooth — avoid ice, hard candies and chewing pen caps.
Alcohol: avoid for at least 72 hours after surgery as it interferes with healing and can interact with antibiotics.

sections.heading: Managing Pain: Medications and Comfort Tips

blocks.text: Dental implant surgery is performed under local anaesthesia and is not painful during the procedure. Post-operative discomfort is typically described as pressure and mild to moderate achiness — rarely severe pain. For most single-tooth implant cases, alternating 400–600 mg ibuprofen with 500 mg acetaminophen every four hours (staggered, not taken together) provides excellent control. Dr. Kadivar will prescribe something stronger if your case warrants it.

Beyond medication, several strategies reduce discomfort: keeping your head elevated when resting, applying ice as instructed, eating only soft foods, and avoiding any strenuous activity for the first three to five days. Psychological state also matters — patients who are well-informed and feel prepared before surgery consistently report lower perceived pain levels than those who feel anxious going in.

sections.heading: When You Can Return to Normal Activity

blocks.text: Most patients with desk or light office work return within one to two days. More physical jobs — construction, nursing, teaching — may require three to five days away. Exercise should be avoided for at least five to seven days: elevated heart rate and blood pressure increase bleeding risk, and sweating in a gym environment increases infection risk while the surgical site is open.

Flying in an airplane within the first three days is generally fine for single-tooth implants, but check with Dr. Kadivar if you had bone grafting or a sinus lift — altitude changes can temporarily cause sinus pressure that is uncomfortable in these cases. Travel plans are worth discussing at your pre-operative appointment so you can time surgery appropriately.

title: Dental Bridge vs. Dental Implant: Which Lasts Longer?
seoTitle: Dental Bridge vs. Dental Implant: Which Lasts Longer? | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Choosing between a dental bridge and an implant in Markham? Compare longevity, cost, bone health impact and candidacy to make the right decision for your smile.
excerpt: Bridges and implants both replace a single missing tooth, but they differ fundamentally in how they work and how long they last. A bridge lasts 10–15 years; an implant is designed for a lifetime. Here is the full comparison.
intro: When a single tooth needs replacing, two options dominate the conversation: a dental bridge and a dental implant. A bridge is faster to complete and has a lower upfront cost — which is why many patients gravitate toward it initially. But bridges also require grinding down the two healthy teeth on either side to anchor the restoration, and they do nothing to prevent the bone loss that begins the moment a tooth root is gone.

This guide walks through every meaningful difference between bridges and implants: lifespan, cost over time, bone health, the procedure experience, and which type of patient typically benefits most from each. If you are weighing this decision in Markham, read through each section and then [book a consultation](/appointments) with Dr. Kadivar for a personalised recommendation.

sections.heading: How Each Option Works

blocks.text: A **dental bridge** spans the gap left by a missing tooth by anchoring to the teeth on either side (called abutment teeth). These abutment teeth are ground down by roughly 60–70 percent of their natural structure to accept the crowns that hold the bridge. The result is three connected crowns — one fake tooth (pontic) flanked by two real-tooth crowns — that are cemented permanently in place. The bridge sits above the gum line with no contact between the pontic and the jawbone.

A **dental implant** replaces the missing tooth from root to crown. A titanium post is placed surgically into the jawbone; once osseointegration is complete, a standalone crown is placed on top. The implant is entirely independent of neighbouring teeth — they are not touched. The root-like post stimulates the jawbone exactly as a natural root would, preventing bone loss at the extraction site. See the full [dental implants cost and process guide](/blog/dental-implants-markham-cost-process) for a step-by-step overview.

sections.heading: Longevity: The Clearest Difference

blocks.text: A well-maintained dental bridge typically lasts 10–15 years before needing replacement. The most common reasons for failure are decay under one of the anchor crowns (because the junction between crown and tooth is hard to clean), failure of the cement that bonds the bridge, or mechanical fracture of the porcelain. When a bridge fails, it usually means replacing the entire three-unit restoration — and sometimes the abutment teeth beneath it have deteriorated enough to require additional treatment.

A dental implant has a projected lifespan of 25 years or more for the titanium post, with studies showing survival rates above 90 percent at 20 years. The crown on top may need replacement after 15–25 years, but this is a relatively minor procedure compared to bridge replacement. Over a 30-year period, a patient will typically replace a bridge two to three times; the implant post may never need replacement at all.

items: Dental bridge: average lifespan 10–15 years; two to three replacements over a lifetime.
Dental implant post: designed for lifetime function; survival rates above 90% at 20 years.
Implant crown: 15–25 years before potential replacement — a minor procedure.
Bridge failure risk: increased by decay under anchor crowns, which is difficult to prevent.
Implant failure risk: primarily peri-implantitis (preventable with diligent oral hygiene).

sections.heading: The Damage to Adjacent Teeth

blocks.text: The most significant long-term cost of a dental bridge is what it does to the two healthy teeth on either side of the gap. Removing 60–70 percent of a tooth's natural structure to create a crown significantly weakens that tooth and makes it permanently dependent on the crown for protection. Crowned teeth are more likely to develop decay at the margins, require root canals if the nerve is irritated by preparation, and may eventually need extraction — creating a cascade of additional treatment.

A dental implant, by contrast, leaves adjacent teeth entirely untouched. Their enamel, dentin and nerve remain intact. This is particularly important when the teeth on either side of the gap are young, healthy and have never had restorations — grinding them down unnecessarily is a significant trade-off that many patients later regret once they understand what was involved.

sections.heading: Bone Loss: The Hidden Problem with Bridges

blocks.text: Because a bridge pontic sits above the gum and does not contact the jawbone, it does not stimulate bone at the extraction site. The bone beneath it continues to resorb over time, just as it would if the gap were left empty. This gradual resorption is visible over years: the bridge may start to show a gap between the pontic and the gum as the tissue and bone settle downward, requiring the bridge to be remade to close the gap.

This bone loss also has practical consequences if the bridge eventually fails and you want an implant: you may not have enough bone left for implant placement without [bone grafting](/blog/bone-grafting-before-implants). Choosing the implant from the start preserves that bone permanently, keeping your options open and avoiding future grafting costs. Read more about [what happens if you wait too long to replace a missing tooth](/blog/waiting-to-replace-missing-tooth).

sections.heading: Cost Comparison: Upfront vs. Lifetime

blocks.text: A three-unit dental bridge in Markham typically costs $2,500–$4,500 — significantly less than a single-tooth implant at $3,000–$6,000. If budget is the primary constraint, a bridge offers a lower initial investment. However, over a 30-year period the bridge will likely need replacement two to three times, with each replacement running $2,500–$5,000 (costs increase if the anchor teeth have deteriorated). The lifetime cost of three bridge replacements can easily exceed $12,000–$15,000.

The lifetime cost of an implant — post placement, crown, and a possible crown replacement in 20 years — typically runs $5,000–$9,000 over 30 years, with no damage to adjacent teeth factored in. When total expenditure over a lifetime is the metric, implants are usually more cost-effective than bridges for most patients under age 65.

sections.heading: When Is a Bridge the Better Choice?

blocks.text: Bridges are appropriate — and sometimes preferable — in specific situations. If the adjacent teeth on either side of the gap already have large fillings, cracked enamel or other restorative needs, crowning them as part of a bridge treatment makes clinical sense: you are improving teeth that needed attention anyway. Patients with insufficient bone for an implant who are not candidates for grafting, or those with medical contraindications to surgery, may find a bridge is the most practical option.

Bridges also have a significantly shorter treatment timeline — typically two to three appointments over two to four weeks compared to the three-to-twelve-month implant process. For patients who need a tooth replaced quickly before an important life event, or who have a strong preference for avoiding surgery, a bridge may be more suitable.

sections.heading: Making the Decision in Markham

blocks.text: At [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/dental-implants), every patient considering tooth replacement receives a thorough evaluation that includes 3D imaging, a review of adjacent tooth health, and a side-by-side cost and longevity comparison for the options relevant to their specific case. There is no pressure toward either option — the goal is the choice that serves you best across your entire lifespan.

The [Canadian Dental Association](https://www.cda-adc.ca/) recognises both bridges and implants as viable tooth-replacement options, and the right choice depends on your clinical situation. [Book a consultation](/appointments) with Dr. Neda Kadivar in Markham to get a personalised recommendation, written cost comparison and timeline estimate.

Ontario Dental Association

title: What Happens If You Wait Too Long to Replace a Missing Tooth?
seoTitle: What Happens If You Wait to Replace a Missing Tooth? | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Delaying tooth replacement causes bone loss, shifting teeth and bite problems. Learn what happens month by month and why early treatment matters in Markham.
excerpt: A missing tooth might feel like an aesthetic problem — especially if it is not visible — but the consequences of leaving it untreated start immediately and compound over time. Bone loss, shifting teeth and bite collapse are all preventable if you act early.
intro: It is tempting to put off replacing a missing tooth, particularly if it is in a location that nobody else notices. The tooth is gone, the pain has stopped, and life goes on — so what is the hurry? The answer is that the jawbone beneath an empty socket begins resorbing immediately after extraction, and the surrounding teeth begin drifting toward the gap within weeks. What starts as an aesthetic problem becomes a structural and financial one the longer it is left unaddressed.

This article explains the timeline of bone loss and tooth movement following extraction, the downstream consequences for your bite, the remaining teeth and your facial appearance, and why early treatment — ideally with a [dental implant](/dental-implants) — almost always results in a simpler, less expensive outcome than waiting.

sections.heading: What Happens in the First Year After Extraction

blocks.text: Bone loss at an extraction site is rapid in the first year. Research published in dental journals consistently shows that the jawbone at the site of a missing tooth loses approximately **25 percent of its width within the first year**. The height of the bone also decreases, typically by one to two millimetres in the first twelve months. This resorption happens because bone is a living tissue that responds to the mechanical stimulation of chewing forces — without a tooth root to stimulate it, the body begins reabsorbing the bone as no longer necessary.

At the same time, the adjacent teeth begin to drift into the space. This movement is usually slow — fractions of a millimetre per month — but it is continuous and eventually visible on an x-ray. The tooth directly behind the gap typically tips forward; the tooth above or below (the opposing tooth) super-erupts downward or upward into the space as it loses its opposing contact. Together these movements create bite irregularities and can expose previously protected tooth surfaces to wear and decay.

sections.heading: Years 2–5: Compounding Problems

blocks.text: By year two or three, bone loss has continued and the adjacent teeth have moved enough to close the gap partially. This creates a new problem: the space that was originally the correct size for an implant crown is now too narrow, or the bite relationship between upper and lower teeth has changed enough to complicate restoration. A patient who could have had a straightforward single-tooth implant in year one may now need orthodontic treatment to reopen the space before an implant can be placed.

Drifted teeth also create new decay risk. When teeth shift out of their natural position, the contact points between adjacent teeth change, creating new food-trap areas where floss once glided through easily. Cavities at these new contact areas are common in patients who have had untreated gaps for several years. The opposing tooth that has super-erupted may now contact its opposing tooth at an angle, causing accelerated wear on both.

Key insight: Every month of delay after extraction slightly complicates future treatment. Bone grafting, orthodontic space maintenance and bite correction are all costs that may have been avoided entirely with timely implant placement.

sections.heading: The Effect on Facial Appearance

blocks.text: The jawbone gives your face its shape. When bone is lost following tooth extraction, the soft tissue — gum, cheek and lip — gradually follows. In the short term, the gum line at the extraction site recedes slightly. Over years, significant bone loss can create visible changes to the contour of the lower face: the cheeks appear less full, the chin may seem to protrude slightly relative to a receding upper jaw, and deep lines can appear around the mouth earlier than normal aging would produce.

Patients who wore conventional dentures for many years before switching to implants often remark on the dramatic change in their facial profile after implant placement — because the implants halt further bone loss and, in conjunction with the prosthetic, restore some of the lost volume. Choosing implants earlier in the tooth-loss journey preserves that bone and the facial structure that depends on it.

sections.heading: How Waiting Affects Future Implant Treatment

blocks.text: Implants require sufficient bone volume for the titanium post to integrate. When patients wait years before pursuing implant treatment, they often find they no longer have the bone depth or width for standard implant placement. This is not a dead end — [bone grafting](/blog/bone-grafting-before-implants) can rebuild lost bone — but it adds three to six months and $800–$2,500+ to the treatment before the implant can even be placed. A sinus lift, if needed for an upper jaw with insufficient height, adds further time and cost.

There are also limits to how much bone can be regenerated. Patients who have had extensive bone loss over many years may not be candidates for standard individual implants at all, leaving them with only [All-on-4 implants](/blog/all-on-4-implants-markham) or [implant-supported dentures](/dental-implants/implant-dentures) as implant options — which, while excellent solutions, are considerably more involved and expensive than a single-tooth implant.

sections.heading: How Soon Should You Replace a Missing Tooth?

blocks.text: The ideal window for implant placement is **two to four months after extraction**, once the extraction socket has healed but bone loss has been minimal. In some cases — when the extraction site is free of infection and bone is sufficient — immediate implant placement on the same day as extraction is possible. This eliminates the waiting period entirely and some patients leave with a temporary crown that same day.

If you are not yet a candidate for an implant — for example, because you are still in active orthodontic treatment, or a systemic condition needs stabilisation first — your dentist may place a space maintainer to prevent drifting while you wait. The key is not to let the socket simply sit without any plan, as each passing month narrows your future options.

items: Immediate implant (same-day extraction): optimal if bone and soft tissue allow it.
Early implant (2–4 months post-extraction): most common timing; minimal bone loss has occurred.
Standard implant (6–12 months): bone loss has begun; a 3D scan will show whether grafting is needed.
Late implant (1+ years): often requires bone grafting; drifted teeth may need orthodontic correction first.
Very late implant (3+ years): significant grafting likely; may limit which implant types are possible.

sections.heading: What If You Have Already Waited?

blocks.text: If you have already waited months or years since losing a tooth, the situation is not hopeless — it simply requires a more thorough assessment. A 3D cone-beam CT scan at Smile Dental Arts Centre will show exactly how much bone remains, where adjacent teeth have moved, and what the options are for restoring the site. Many patients who present years after an extraction are still excellent implant candidates after bone grafting.

The important thing is not to let the fact that you have already waited become a reason to wait longer. Every additional month of bone loss and tooth drift makes future treatment slightly more complex. [Book a consultation](/appointments) with Dr. Kadivar and let the 3D imaging tell you exactly where you stand — you may be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward the solution still is.

sections.heading: Prevention: Socket Preservation at Time of Extraction

blocks.text: If you are about to have a tooth extracted and are not yet ready for immediate implant placement, ask your dentist about **socket preservation** (also called alveolar ridge preservation). A bone grafting material is packed into the socket immediately after extraction to prevent or slow the bone resorption that would otherwise occur. This procedure adds modest cost and a brief recovery, but it significantly preserves bone volume — making future implant placement simpler and often avoiding the need for a larger graft later.

At Smile Dental Arts Centre, we routinely discuss socket preservation with every patient who is having a tooth extracted and plans to pursue an implant eventually but not immediately. The conversation takes a few minutes; the bone it preserves can save months of grafting time and hundreds or thousands of dollars in treatment cost.
