Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario

title: TMJ Pain and Your Bite: When to See a Dentist
seoTitle: TMJ Pain and Your Bite: When to See a Dentist | Smile Dental Arts Centre Markham
metaDescription: Clicking jaw, morning headaches, difficulty chewing — these are signs of TMJ disorder. Learn how bite alignment contributes to TMJ pain and when to seek dental care in Markham.
excerpt: The temporomandibular joint is one of the most complex joints in the body, and when it is under chronic strain — often from a misaligned bite or bruxism — the symptoms can include jaw pain, clicking, headaches and neck tension. This article explains the connection and what treatment can help.
intro: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) connects your lower jaw to your skull on each side of your face. It is active in virtually every function of the oral cavity: chewing, speaking, yawning, swallowing. When this joint is under chronic strain — whether from a bite that is not well-aligned, from grinding and clenching, or from injury — the resulting symptoms can range from mild jaw discomfort to debilitating pain that extends into the face, head and neck.

This article explains what causes TMJ disorder, how bite alignment relates to joint health, what symptoms warrant a dental evaluation, and what treatment options are available at [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/appointments) in Markham.

sections.heading: Understanding the Temporomandibular Joint

blocks.text: The TMJ is a hinge-and-sliding joint — it both rotates (when you open slightly) and translates forward (when you open wide). A small cartilage disc sits between the ball of the lower jaw and the socket in the skull, cushioning the joint during all these movements. Ligaments stabilise the joint; a group of muscles — the masseter, temporalis, pterygoids and others — control its movement and bear the forces of chewing, which can reach over 100 pounds per square inch on the back teeth.

Because the TMJ operates continuously throughout every waking hour, and often throughout the night for patients who clench or grind, it is susceptible to cumulative strain. Small imbalances — a bite that causes the jaw to deviate slightly to one side to close, for example — translate into thousands of slightly asymmetric joint movements per day, gradually irritating the joint, the disc and the surrounding soft tissue.

sections.heading: How Bite Misalignment Contributes to TMJ Problems

blocks.text: When the upper and lower teeth do not occlude (meet) evenly, the jaw must shift into an unnatural position to achieve maximum tooth contact for chewing. This shift is unconscious — the neuromuscular system adapts automatically to bring as many teeth into contact as possible. The problem is that achieving maximum tooth contact by shifting the jaw also means the TMJ is not in its most anatomically ideal position, creating chronic strain on the joint and the muscles that hold the jaw in that adapted position.

Common bite problems that stress the TMJ include: significant overbite (deep bite), underbite, crossbite, and missing teeth that have allowed adjacent teeth to drift and change the bite. Orthodontic correction — through [Invisalign](/blog/invisalign-markham-cost-timeline) or traditional braces — addresses the root cause in these cases and often produces meaningful improvement in TMJ symptoms once the bite is corrected.

sections.heading: Recognising TMJ Disorder Symptoms

blocks.text: TMJ disorder (also called temporomandibular disorder or TMD) produces a range of symptoms that patients do not always associate with their jaw. The classic presentation includes jaw pain or tenderness, especially on waking, and clicking or popping sounds when opening or closing the mouth. The sounds alone, without pain, are common and not always clinically significant — it is the combination of sound with pain, locking, or limited opening that warrants evaluation.

items: Jaw pain or tenderness on one or both sides, especially on waking.
Clicking, popping or grating sounds in the jaw joint when opening or closing.
Limited jaw opening — inability to open as wide as normal without pain.
Jaw locking — momentary inability to fully open or close the jaw.
Headaches at the temples, behind the eyes or at the base of the skull.
Ear pain, fullness or ringing (tinnitus) without a clear ear cause.
Neck and shoulder tension that worsens with jaw clenching.

sections.heading: The Role of Bruxism in TMJ Strain

blocks.text: Bruxism — the habitual grinding and clenching of teeth — is one of the most significant drivers of TMJ disorder. During sleep, clenching forces can reach two to three times those of normal chewing, applied continuously for hours. The muscles involved become chronically overworked, developing the same kind of tension and soreness that skeletal muscles develop after prolonged exercise. Morning jaw soreness and temporal headaches are classic signatures of nocturnal bruxism.

A custom night guard is the most effective way to protect the joint and teeth from bruxism forces during sleep. It reduces the muscle activity of clenching and prevents the enamel-on-enamel contact that damages teeth over time. If bruxism is also driven by a bite misalignment, addressing the bite issue with orthodontics — including [Invisalign](/dental-services) — may reduce the grinding trigger itself. For more on the night guard side of this discussion, see our [night guards vs. Invisalign article](/blog/night-guards-vs-invisalign).

sections.heading: When to See a Dentist for Jaw Pain

blocks.text: Not every jaw click requires treatment — isolated, painless clicking is common and often benign. However, you should seek a dental evaluation when: jaw pain persists beyond a few days, clicking is accompanied by pain or limited opening, you wake regularly with jaw or temple soreness, or your jaw locks or catches during normal function. Early evaluation allows for conservative treatment before the condition progresses.

If your dentist suspects TMJ disorder they will examine the joint directly — palpating the muscles and joint for tenderness, measuring jaw opening, listening for joint sounds and assessing your bite. X-rays show the bony structures; occasionally an MRI is needed to visualise the cartilage disc. Most TMJ cases are managed by dentists without specialist referral, though complex cases involving significant disc displacement may benefit from evaluation by an oral and maxillofacial specialist.

sections.heading: Treatment Options for TMJ Disorder

blocks.text: The great majority of TMJ disorder cases resolve or improve significantly with conservative treatment. **Night guards** reduce clenching forces and allow the muscles and joint to rest during sleep. **Physiotherapy** targeting the jaw muscles — including stretching exercises, heat therapy and manual release techniques — is highly effective for muscle-dominant TMD. **Anti-inflammatory medication** (ibuprofen) during acute flares reduces pain and inflammation. **Stress management** matters enormously: anxiety and stress are major drivers of clenching, and addressing the psychological component produces meaningful clinical improvement.

When bite misalignment is a clear contributing factor, orthodontic treatment is appropriate. When missing teeth have caused bite collapse, dental restoration (including implants, crowns or dentures) addresses the underlying structural problem. Surgical intervention is rarely necessary and is reserved for disc displacement that does not respond to conservative treatment.

sections.heading: Getting Evaluated in Markham

blocks.text: Dr. Neda Kadivar has significant experience in diagnosing and managing TMJ disorder in the context of overall bite health. At Smile Dental Arts Centre, a TMJ evaluation includes a comprehensive bite analysis, muscle palpation, a review of your symptom history and — where orthodontic issues are suspected — a ClinCheck simulation showing what bite correction would involve. Treatment plans are conservative and sequenced: the simplest effective intervention first, with escalation only if needed.

[Book an appointment](/appointments) in Markham if you are experiencing any of the symptoms described above. TMJ problems that are addressed early respond much better to conservative treatment than those that have been present for years. We are available Monday through Friday with extended evening hours and every other Saturday.

title: How Much Does Invisalign Really Cost After Insurance?
seoTitle: Invisalign Cost After Insurance in Ontario | Smile Dental Arts Centre Markham
metaDescription: Wondering what Invisalign costs out-of-pocket after insurance in Ontario? Learn what plans typically cover, how to maximise your benefit and what financing options are available.
excerpt: Most Ontario dental plans include an orthodontic benefit that significantly reduces Invisalign costs — but understanding what you will actually pay out-of-pocket requires knowing exactly how your plan works. This guide breaks it down clearly.
intro: The headline price for Invisalign in Markham is typically $3,000 to $7,500 — but for most patients with employer-sponsored dental benefits, the actual out-of-pocket cost is considerably lower. Ontario group dental plans almost universally include an orthodontic benefit, and that benefit applies to Invisalign just as it applies to traditional braces, making the choice between the two a matter of clinical fit rather than insurance penalty.

This guide explains exactly how orthodontic insurance benefits work in Ontario, what a typical benefit covers and what it leaves uncovered, how to read your benefit booklet, and what financing options are available at [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/appointments) for the remaining balance after insurance.

sections.heading: How Orthodontic Insurance Benefits Work

blocks.text: Orthodontic benefits in Ontario group plans typically operate differently from regular dental benefits. Rather than covering a percentage of each appointment, orthodontic benefits are usually paid as a percentage of the total treatment fee — commonly 50 percent — up to a lifetime maximum per covered person. The lifetime maximum is the most important number to know: it applies once per covered person for their lifetime under the plan, not per year.

For example, a plan with 50 percent coverage and a $2,500 lifetime orthodontic maximum would pay $2,500 toward a $5,000 Invisalign case — leaving $2,500 out of pocket. Orthodontic benefits are paid in installments over the course of active treatment rather than in a lump sum: the insurer typically pays a portion at the start of treatment and the remainder in equal monthly or quarterly installments as treatment progresses.

sections.heading: Does Insurance Cover Invisalign Specifically?

blocks.text: Yes — virtually all Ontario dental plans that include orthodontic benefits cover Invisalign on equal terms with traditional braces. The [Canadian Dental Association](https://www.cda-adc.ca/) codes used for comprehensive orthodontic treatment do not specify the appliance type, and insurers do not differentiate between Invisalign and braces for reimbursement purposes. If your plan covers braces, it covers Invisalign for the same amount.

The only scenario where Invisalign-specific exclusions appear is in very old legacy benefit booklets written before Invisalign became mainstream — and even these are increasingly rare. If you have any doubt, call your insurer directly and ask: does the orthodontic benefit apply equally to clear aligner treatment such as Invisalign? Get the answer in writing or reference number format.

sections.heading: What Plans Typically Do Not Cover

blocks.text: While the orthodontic benefit covers the main Invisalign treatment fee, several related costs may fall outside the benefit: the initial consultation fee (if charged separately), records fees for x-rays and digital scans, replacement aligners beyond those included in the manufacturer's replacement policy, and retainers at the end of treatment. Some plans include retainers within the orthodontic benefit; others treat them as a prosthetic and cover them under a different section; still others exclude them.

Understanding these potential gaps before treatment begins allows you to budget accurately. At our Markham clinic, the treatment coordinator prepares a written estimate showing the all-inclusive treatment fee, the expected insurance contribution based on your specific benefit, and your estimated out-of-pocket balance — before you sign any treatment agreement.

items: Lifetime orthodontic maximum — the single most important number; typically $1,500–$3,500.
Percentage covered — usually 50% of eligible fees up to the lifetime maximum.
Waiting periods — some plans have 12–24 month waits for new enrollees.
Age limits — some plans cover orthodontics only for dependents under age 18 or 21.
Retainers — check whether your plan covers retainers within the orthodontic benefit or separately.

sections.heading: Coordinating Two Plans (Dual Coverage)

blocks.text: Patients who have coverage under two plans — for example, their own employer plan and their spouse's employer plan — can coordinate benefits to significantly reduce out-of-pocket costs. In dual coverage, the primary plan pays first up to its lifetime maximum; the secondary plan then pays a portion of the remaining balance. Combined, dual coverage can sometimes cover 80–100 percent of Invisalign costs for patients whose plans have generous lifetime orthodontic maximums.

Our billing team is experienced in coordinating dual orthodontic coverage and will manage the submission to both insurers on your behalf. Bring benefit cards for both plans to your consultation so we can run a benefit check on both before developing your financial plan.

sections.heading: The Canadian Dental Care Plan and Orthodontics

blocks.text: The federal [Canadian Dental Care Plan](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/dental/dental-care-plan.html) is available to households with adjusted net family income below $90,000 who do not have access to private dental insurance. The CDCP covers some orthodontic services for children and youth, though the scope and fee schedule for orthodontics under this program continues to evolve. If your household qualifies for the CDCP, bring your benefit card to your consultation and we will run a benefit check to determine what is covered.

Adult orthodontics under the CDCP is more limited; coverage in this area is primarily focused on preventing functional problems rather than elective aesthetic treatment. However, cases where misalignment causes documented functional difficulty may qualify for some coverage even for adult patients. Our administrative team stays current on CDCP updates and will advise you on the latest eligibility criteria.

sections.heading: Financing the Out-of-Pocket Balance

blocks.text: After applying insurance benefits, many patients still have an out-of-pocket balance ranging from $500 to $4,000+ depending on case complexity and plan generosity. Our Markham clinic offers in-office payment plans with no interest for balances paid within 12 months, and referrals to dental financing providers offering extended terms of 24–60 months. Monthly payments on a $2,500 balance over 24 months are typically around $100 — manageable alongside other household expenses.

Patients who are self-employed or who have a health spending account (HSA) through their employer can use those funds to pay for Invisalign with pre-tax money. Dental expenses not reimbursed by insurance are also eligible for the federal Medical Expense Tax Credit, which can return meaningful dollars in tax savings for patients in higher income brackets.

sections.heading: Getting Your Insurance Picture Clarified Before You Start

blocks.text: The most empowering thing you can do before beginning Invisalign is to get a pre-determination from your insurer. Our clinic submits pre-determinations on behalf of every orthodontic patient — you will receive a written response from your insurer specifying exactly what they will pay toward your treatment before we make your first aligner. This eliminates billing surprises and allows you to plan your finances with accuracy.

[Book an Invisalign consultation](/appointments) at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham and bring your benefit card. We will run the benefit check, show you your ClinCheck smile simulation, and give you a complete financial picture — all at the same appointment. There is no obligation to proceed, and there is no guessing.

title: Retainers After Invisalign: How to Keep Your Results
seoTitle: Retainers After Invisalign: Keeping Your Results | Smile Dental Arts Centre Markham
metaDescription: Orthodontic results do not last without retainers. Learn the types of retainers available, how long to wear them, how to care for them and what happens if you stop.
excerpt: Teeth moved during Invisalign treatment will relapse — shift back toward their original positions — if retainers are not worn consistently after treatment. This guide explains the retention options, the wear schedule, and how to protect your investment for life.
intro: Finishing your last Invisalign aligner is an exciting milestone. But the end of active treatment is not the end of the process — it is the beginning of the retention phase, which is what keeps your teeth in their new positions permanently. Without consistent retainer wear, orthodontic relapse is essentially inevitable: the periodontal fibres that anchor teeth in bone have memory and will gradually pull teeth back toward their pre-treatment positions.

This article explains why retention is non-negotiable, the retainer options available at [Smile Dental Arts Centre](/appointments) after Invisalign, how long and how often retainers need to be worn, and how to care for removable retainers over the years. If you have questions about retainers before your Invisalign treatment concludes, see our [Invisalign Markham guide](/blog/invisalign-markham-cost-timeline) for the full treatment picture.

sections.heading: Why Teeth Move After Orthodontic Treatment

blocks.text: During Invisalign treatment, aligner forces gradually move teeth through the bone. The bone remodels around the new tooth positions — dissolving on the pressure side and forming on the tension side. But this remodelling takes time to fully mature: for months after active treatment ends, the bone around the teeth is not yet fully mineralised, and the periodontal ligament fibres that attach the tooth to the bone retain their pre-treatment orientation and tension.

These immature fibres exert a pull on the teeth toward their old positions — a process called orthodontic relapse. The front teeth — particularly lower incisors — are the most susceptible to relapse because they are narrow, multiple, and subject to tongue pressure. Upper front teeth are typically more stable but still require retention. Without a retainer to counteract this pull, teeth will begin moving within weeks of completing Invisalign.

sections.heading: Types of Retainers

blocks.text: There are three main types of retainers, each with different characteristics. **Clear removable retainers** (like Vivera retainers made by Invisalign, or similar Essix-style retainers) look almost identical to Invisalign aligners. They are the most common choice after Invisalign because patients are already accustomed to clear tray wear. They are worn full-time for the first few months, then transitioned to nights-only wear. They need to be replaced every two to five years as the plastic ages.

items: **Clear removable retainer (Essix/Vivera):** most discreet, easy to wear, requires replacement every 2–5 years.
**Hawley retainer (wire and acrylic):** more durable, adjustable, allows teeth to settle into natural contact; more visible.
**Bonded/permanent retainer:** thin wire glued to the back of the lower (and sometimes upper) front teeth; maintenance-free, cannot be forgotten.
**Combination:** bonded wire for lower front teeth + clear retainer for upper arch is a popular approach at our clinic.
**Night guard retainer:** for patients who grind, a hard acrylic appliance that functions as both retainer and bruxism guard.

sections.heading: The Retention Wear Schedule

blocks.text: Dr. Kadivar prescribes a retention schedule based on your specific case. The standard protocol for clear removable retainers is: full-time wear (20–22 hours per day, removing only to eat and brush) for the first three to six months after active treatment ends. After this initial phase, nightly wear — every night without exception — is recommended indefinitely. The phrase often used is: wear your retainer as long as you want to keep your teeth straight.

Patients sometimes ask whether they can eventually stop wearing retainers at all. The honest answer is that after several years of consistent nighttime wear, many patients find they can reduce to four to five nights per week without perceptible relapse — but completely stopping, even after ten years, carries relapse risk. Teeth continue to experience natural forces throughout life, and some degree of retention is needed to counteract these forces indefinitely.

sections.heading: Caring for Removable Retainers

blocks.text: Clear retainer care is essentially identical to [Invisalign aligner care](/blog/how-to-care-for-invisalign-trays): rinse in cool water every time you remove them, brush gently with clear soap morning and evening, soak weekly in retainer cleaning solution, and store in the case provided when not in your mouth. The same rules apply — no hot water (warps the plastic), no toothpaste (scratches the surface), no coloured beverages while wearing.

Clear retainers develop micro-cracks and discolouration over time and will eventually need replacement. On average, a clear retainer lasts two to five years with proper care. Keep an eye on the fit: if the retainer no longer seats fully — if it feels like it is not quite covering the teeth completely — the retainer may have warped, or minor tooth movement may have occurred. Report either scenario to Dr. Kadivar promptly.

Replacement tip: Order a replacement retainer before your current one fails, not after. If your retainer breaks and you have no replacement, teeth can shift meaningfully within weeks. Many patients order a backup set of retainers at the completion of Invisalign and store them safely for exactly this situation.

sections.heading: Bonded Retainers: The Set-It-and-Forget-It Option

blocks.text: A bonded (permanent) retainer is a thin, flexible wire cemented to the back (lingual) surfaces of the front teeth — typically the lower four to six incisors, and sometimes the upper front teeth. Once placed, it cannot be removed by the patient and works continuously without any thought or compliance required. For patients who know they are unlikely to remember to wear a removable retainer consistently, a bonded retainer eliminates the relapse risk from forgotten wear.

Bonded retainers require some attention to hygiene: flossing requires a floss threader to pass the floss under the wire, and the wire must be cleaned thoroughly at every brushing. At professional cleaning appointments, the hygienist checks the wire for any detached bonding points — a partially debonded wire no longer holds the tooth and can actually push it out of position. Dr. Kadivar checks bonded retainers at every recall examination.

sections.heading: What Happens If You Stop Wearing Your Retainer?

blocks.text: The severity of relapse depends on how long retainers were worn before stopping, which teeth were moved, and individual biology. Lower front teeth are the first to show relapse, typically beginning within weeks of stopping retainer wear. The relapse is usually slowest in the first year and then accelerates as the periodontal fibres mature in their pre-treatment orientation.

If you have stopped wearing your retainer and notice your teeth shifting, contact Dr. Kadivar as soon as possible. Early relapse — within the first few months — may be addressed by a new retainer that applies gentle pressure to return teeth to their corrected positions. Significant relapse that has progressed over months or years may require a short course of refinement aligners to re-correct the movement, adding cost and time that consistent retainer wear would have prevented entirely.

sections.heading: Protecting Your Investment Long-Term

blocks.text: The Invisalign investment you made — financially and in terms of the months spent wearing aligners — is worth protecting. The cost of consistent retainer replacement over a lifetime is a small fraction of the cost of retreatment. Think of nighttime retainer wear as maintenance for your smile in the same way oil changes are maintenance for a car: routine, simple and vastly less expensive than the alternative.

At Smile Dental Arts Centre, we review your retainer fit at every regular dental examination so any issues are caught early. If you have lost or broken your retainer, [call us at (905) 604-7330](/contact-us) or [book online](/appointments) — we will arrange a replacement as quickly as possible to minimise any tooth movement during the gap.

title: Signs You Might Need a Root Canal
seoTitle: Signs You Might Need a Root Canal | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Not sure if your tooth needs a root canal? Learn the common warning signs, what they mean, and when to see a dentist in Markham. A clear, patient-friendly guide.
primaryKeyword: signs you need a root canal
excerpt: Not sure if your tooth needs a root canal? Learn the common warning signs, what they mean, and when to see a dentist in Markham. A clear, patient-friendly guide.
intro: If a tooth has been nagging you, the honest short answer is this: a root canal becomes likely when the soft tissue inside the tooth — the pulp — is inflamed or infected and cannot recover on its own. You usually cannot confirm that yourself, but a handful of symptoms make it far more probable, and a few of them mean you should be seen quickly.

This article walks through the warning signs one by one, explains what each tends to indicate, and tells you which ones can wait a few days and which cannot. It is general information, not a diagnosis — only an in-person exam and X-rays can confirm what your tooth actually needs.

sections.heading: First, what a root canal is actually for

blocks.text: Every tooth contains a small chamber of living tissue: nerves, blood vessels and connective tissue, together called the pulp. When decay, a crack or an injury lets bacteria reach the pulp, it can become inflamed and then infected. Once that inflammation passes a certain point, the pulp does not heal — it dies, and infection can spread out through the root tip into the surrounding bone.

A root canal removes that damaged pulp, disinfects the inside of the tooth and seals it, so the tooth can stay in your mouth instead of being pulled. If you want the full step-by-step, we cover it in [what happens during a root canal](/blog/what-happens-during-a-root-canal). Here, we are focused on the *signals* that this might be where you are headed.

sections.heading: The most common warning signs

blocks.text: No single symptom proves you need treatment, and some people have several at once while others have almost none. Look at the overall picture rather than any one item.
1. Pain that lingers, throbs, or wakes you up

Ordinary twinges come and go. Pulp problems tend to produce pain that hangs around — a deep, throbbing ache, pain that builds over hours, or a toothache that wakes you at night or worsens when you lie down. Spontaneous pain (hurting for no obvious reason) is a classic sign that the pulp is irritated beyond the point of recovery.
2. Sensitivity to hot or cold that does not settle

Feeling a jolt from ice water is normal and fades in a second or two. The concerning pattern is sensitivity that *lingers* for many seconds or minutes after the hot or cold source is gone, or heat sensitivity that makes you reach for cold water for relief. That lasting response points toward the pulp rather than everyday sensitivity — we explain the difference in [sensitivity to hot and cold that lingers](/blog/lingering-tooth-sensitivity-hot-cold).
3. Pain when you bite or chew

A tooth that hurts specifically under pressure — when you bite, chew on that side, or press it — can indicate that inflammation has reached the tissues around the root, or that the tooth is cracked. Because there are several possible causes, we look at them separately in [tooth pain when you chew](/blog/tooth-pain-when-chewing).
4. A swelling, a "pimple" on the gum, or a bad taste

Swelling of the gum or face, tenderness in the surrounding tissue, or a small recurring bump on the gum that leaks and gives a salty or foul taste all suggest infection has escaped the tooth. The gum bump is a drainage point called a sinus tract; it can appear even when the tooth barely hurts.
5. A tooth that has darkened
A single tooth turning grey, brown or yellow compared with its neighbours can mean the pulp has died, especially after a past knock. Colour change is often painless, which surprises people.
6. A deep cavity, a lost filling, or a cracked tooth

Sometimes the clue is structural rather than a feeling: a large cavity, a filling that has come out, or a visible crack gives bacteria a route to the pulp. Even without much pain, these deserve prompt assessment.
7. Tender, swollen gums around one tooth
Localised gum tenderness and swelling concentrated around a single tooth — rather than general gum soreness — can accompany a pulp that is failing.

sections.heading: Which signs mean "see a dentist urgently"?

blocks.text: Most of the symptoms above warrant a prompt appointment, but a few point to a spreading infection that needs urgent attention rather than a wait-and-see approach:

rows: Facial swelling, especially spreading toward the eye or down the neck
Seek care the same day; if breathing or swallowing is affected, treat it as a medical emergency
Fever with dental pain and swelling
Severe, unrelenting pain not eased by over-the-counter relief
Chronic infection with a drainage tract
Book an assessment soon, even if pain is mild

blocks.text: If any of the urgent signs apply, our [emergency dental care in Markham](/emergency-dentist-markham) page explains how to reach us quickly. Do not wait for a scheduled check-up if your face is swelling or you feel unwell.

sections.heading: Signs that are easy to misread

items: **No pain does not mean no problem.** A pulp can die quietly, and infection can show up on an X-ray before you feel anything. We cover this in [needing a root canal without pain](/blog/root-canal-needed-but-no-pain).
**Pain that suddenly stops is not always good news.** When a badly inflamed pulp finally dies, the pain can ease for a while — even though the underlying problem remains and may flare later.
**Sinus and jaw issues can mimic tooth pain.** Upper back teeth sit near the sinuses, and sinus congestion can feel like a toothache. This is one reason self-diagnosis is unreliable.

sections.heading: How a dentist confirms it

blocks.text: Because symptoms overlap, a dentist does not rely on how the tooth feels alone. Expect a combination of your history, gentle tests (such as cold or tapping tests to compare the tooth with its neighbours) and X-rays to look at the root and surrounding bone. The full picture is what determines whether the pulp can be saved, needs a root canal, or needs another approach. We describe that process in [how dentists diagnose whether you need a root canal](/blog/how-dentists-diagnose-root-canal).

Catching a pulp problem early sometimes means a simpler solution is still possible; leaving it usually narrows the options. If you recognise several of the signs here, an assessment is the sensible next step.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Can a tooth that needs a root canal heal on its own?

Once the pulp is irreversibly inflamed or infected, it does not recover by itself. Symptoms may ease temporarily, but the problem persists. See [will a tooth infection go away on its own](/blog/will-a-tooth-infection-go-away).
How fast do I need to act if I have symptoms but no swelling?
Without urgent signs, it is reasonable to book a prompt appointment rather than treat it as an emergency — but "prompt" means days, not months. Delay tends to reduce your options.
Could my symptoms be something other than a pulp problem?
Yes. A high filling, gum disease, a sinus issue or grinding can all cause similar feelings. That is exactly why an in-person exam matters before assuming you need a root canal.
Does needing a root canal always mean the tooth was neglected?
No. Cracks, trauma and deep decay under old fillings can all reach the pulp even in well-cared-for mouths.

sections.heading: Book an assessment in Markham

blocks.text: If your tooth is sending you these signals, the team at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham can examine it and explain your options clearly. Learn more about [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham) or [request an appointment](/appointments) and we will help you get to the bottom of it.

title: Why Does My Tooth Hurt When I Chew?
seoTitle: Why Your Tooth Hurts When You Chew | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Tooth pain when biting or chewing has several causes — from a high filling to a cracked tooth or pulp problem. Here is how to tell them apart and when to see a dentist.
excerpt: Tooth pain when biting or chewing has several causes — from a high filling to a cracked tooth or pulp problem. Here is how to tell them apart and when to see a dentist.
intro: Pain that shows up only when you bite or chew is a specific clue, and it usually means the problem is either *around* the tooth's root or *within* its structure — not simply on the surface. The most common culprits are a cracked tooth, a bite that lands too hard on one spot, inflammation around the root from a dying pulp, or an abscess. Only an exam can tell which, but the *pattern* of your pain narrows it down more than you might expect.
Below, we sort the usual causes by how they tend to feel, so you can describe your symptoms clearly and know whether to book soon or seek urgent care.

sections.heading: Why chewing pain is different from other toothaches

blocks.text: A tooth sits in bone, cushioned by a thin ligament. When you chew, force travels down the tooth and into that ligament and the bone around the root tip. If those tissues are inflamed — or if the tooth flexes because it is cracked — biting reproduces the pain in a way that hot, cold or sweet foods may not.

That is why "it only hurts when I bite" is worth mentioning specifically to your dentist. It shifts attention toward the root and the tooth's structure, which is different from the surface sensitivity we discuss in [lingering sensitivity to hot and cold](/blog/lingering-tooth-sensitivity-hot-cold).

sections.heading: The usual causes, and how they tend to feel

blocks.text: A cracked or fractured tooth

Cracks often produce a sharp, fleeting pain at the *moment of release* — you bite down, and it zings as you let go. You might notice it only with certain foods or when biting at a particular angle. Cracks can be invisible to the eye and even hard to see on an X-ray, which makes the "pain on release" description valuable. A crack that reaches the pulp can lead to a root canal; one that runs below the gum may not be savable. We go deeper in [cracked tooth and root canal](/blog/cracked-tooth-root-canal).
A "high" filling or crown

If your pain started soon after a new filling or crown, the restoration may sit a fraction too tall, so that tooth hits first when you bite. This concentrates force and irritates the ligament. It is usually an easy adjustment — and a good reason not to assume the worst.
Inflammation around the root (from a failing pulp)

When a pulp becomes infected, the tissue around the root tip can inflame. The tooth may feel tender to tapping and sore to chew on, sometimes with a sensation that it is "raised" or that you notice it before the others meet. Paired with lingering temperature sensitivity or throbbing, this pattern points toward needing a root canal.
A dental abscess

A collection of infection at the root can make the tooth exquisitely tender to any pressure, often with gum swelling, a bad taste, or facial swelling. This one can escalate — see the urgent guidance below and our overview of [dental abscess warning signs](/blog/dental-abscess-warning-signs).
Gum and other causes
Advanced gum disease, food packed between teeth, a loose restoration, or grinding can also make chewing uncomfortable. These are worth ruling out, which is another reason self-diagnosis has limits.

sections.heading: A quick way to describe your pain

blocks.text: Bring these details to your appointment — they genuinely help:

rows: Does it hurt as you bite *down*, or as you *release*?
Pain on release is classic for cracks
Did it start after recent dental work?
Is the tooth tender to tapping or feels "raised"?
Points to inflammation around the root
Any swelling, bad taste, or fever?
Only with certain foods or angles?
Common with cracks and food packing

sections.heading: When to seek care urgently

blocks.text: Book same-day or urgent care if chewing pain comes with facial swelling, fever, a spreading feeling of pressure, or pain you cannot control with over-the-counter relief used as directed. These can indicate a spreading infection. Our [emergency dentist in Markham](/emergency-dentist-markham) page explains how to reach us. Difficulty breathing or swallowing is a medical emergency — seek immediate help.
For pain without those features, a prompt (not emergency) appointment is appropriate. Avoid chewing on that side in the meantime, and keep the area clean.

sections.heading: What the dentist will look for

blocks.text: Expect a bite test (you may be asked to bite on a small prop to find the exact spot and reproduce a crack's pain), gentle tapping to check tenderness, temperature testing to gauge the pulp, and X-rays. Sometimes a crack only reveals itself under magnification or with a special dye. The aim is to find *why* biting hurts before deciding treatment, which might be as simple as an adjustment or as involved as a root canal and crown. For the wider set of warning signs to watch for, see [signs you might need a root canal](/blog/signs-you-need-a-root-canal).

sections.heading: Protecting the tooth until your appointment

blocks.text: Between noticing the pain and being seen, a few simple habits protect the tooth and keep you more comfortable:

items: **Chew on the other side.** Keeping force off the tooth avoids deepening a crack or aggravating inflammation.
**Avoid hard, crunchy and chewy foods** on that side — nuts, hard bread crusts, ice and tough meat all concentrate pressure.
**Ease off temperature extremes** if hot or cold also bother the tooth; lukewarm foods are kinder while you wait.
**Keep the area clean** with gentle brushing, so you are not adding food packing or plaque irritation to the problem.
**Note what triggers the pain** — biting down, releasing, a particular food or angle — and bring that to your appointment.

blocks.text: These measures do not treat the cause, but they buy time without making things worse. If the pain escalates, swelling appears, or you develop a fever, move from "book soon" to "seek urgent care."

sections.heading: When chewing pain is *not* the tooth itself

blocks.text: Occasionally the discomfort you feel on chewing does not come from the tooth you suspect:

items: **Referred pain** — a problem in one tooth can be felt in a neighbour, or upper and lower teeth can be confused, because they share nerve pathways.
**Sinus pressure** — the roots of upper back teeth sit close to the sinuses, so sinus congestion can make several upper teeth ache when you bite or bend forward.
**Clenching and grinding** — overworked jaw muscles and stressed teeth can produce a bite-related soreness that is not decay or infection at all.

blocks.text: None of this is something to sort out yourself, but it is a useful reminder of why an exam beats guesswork: the fix for a high filling, a sinus issue, or a grinding habit is very different from the fix for an infected pulp.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Should I stop eating on that side?
Yes, until you are seen. Chewing on a painful or possibly cracked tooth can worsen a crack or aggravate inflammation.
The pain went away after a day — do I still need to go?
It is wise to be checked. Cracks and pulp problems can quieten temporarily and return, sometimes worse. A brief pain-free spell does not mean the cause has resolved.
Can a high filling really cause this much discomfort?
It can. Even a slightly tall restoration changes how force lands and can make a tooth ache for days until it is adjusted.
Is chewing pain always a root canal?
No. It is often something simpler. But because a few causes are serious, the pattern is worth an exam rather than a guess.

sections.heading: Get it assessed in Markham

blocks.text: If biting or chewing keeps hurting, let us find the cause before it grows. See how we handle [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham) if that turns out to be the issue, or simply [book a visit](/appointments) and we will examine the tooth and explain what is going on.

title: Hot and Cold Sensitivity: When It's Normal and When It Isn't
seoTitle: When Hot & Cold Tooth Sensitivity Signals a Bigger Problem | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: A quick zing from cold is normal; sensitivity that lingers for minutes may not be. Learn how dentists tell everyday sensitivity from a pulp problem — and what to do.
primaryKeyword: lingering tooth sensitivity to hot and cold
excerpt: A quick zing from cold is normal; sensitivity that lingers for minutes may not be. Learn how dentists tell everyday sensitivity from a pulp problem — and what to do.
intro: Here is the distinction that matters most: a brief jolt from something cold that disappears within a second or two is usually ordinary sensitivity, while a reaction that *lingers* for many seconds or minutes — or a tooth that suddenly hurts from heat — is the pattern dentists associate with a pulp that may not recover. The duration and character of the response tell you more than its intensity.
This article helps you read your own symptoms so you can decide whether you are dealing with everyday sensitivity or something that needs a dentist's attention.

sections.heading: Why teeth feel temperature at all

blocks.text: Beneath the enamel lies dentine, threaded with microscopic tubules that connect to the nerve-rich pulp at the tooth's core. When enamel thins or gums recede, hot and cold reach those tubules more easily, and you feel it. That is why sensitivity is so common and usually harmless.

The pulp itself, though, can only respond to irritation in limited ways. When it is mildly irritated it overreacts to temperature but settles quickly — this is often reversible. When it is badly inflamed or dying, the response changes: it lingers, arrives unprompted, or flips so that heat is the trigger. Understanding that shift is the key to this whole topic.

sections.heading: Reversible vs irreversible: the plain-language version

blocks.text: Dentists use two terms worth knowing:

items: **Reversible pulpitis** — the pulp is irritated but still healthy enough to recover. Typical feel: a sharp response to cold or sweet that fades quickly once the trigger is gone. Remove the cause (a cavity, a leaky filling, exposed roots) and the tooth usually calms down. A root canal is often *not* needed. This is the scenario behind [pulp capping and vital pulp therapy](/blog/pulp-capping-vs-root-canal).

**Irreversible pulpitis** — the pulp is inflamed beyond recovery. Typical feel: pain that lingers after the trigger, throbbing, spontaneous aching, or new sensitivity to heat. Here, a root canal (or extraction) is usually the way forward.

blocks.text: You cannot always place yourself neatly in one box, and you should not have to — that is the dentist's job. But the descriptions help you notice which direction your symptoms lean.

sections.heading: Signs your sensitivity is probably harmless

items: A quick, sharp response to cold that vanishes almost immediately.
Sensitivity across several teeth or a whole area, not one specific tooth.
It appears after whitening, a cleaning, or when you have been brushing hard, then improves.
It tracks with exposed root surfaces or general gum recession.

blocks.text: Everyday sensitivity like this often improves with a desensitising toothpaste, a softer brush and gentler technique, and by easing off acidic foods and drinks. If it does not improve over a few weeks, have it checked.

sections.heading: Signs the pulp may be involved

items: Cold or hot pain that **lingers** for 10–30 seconds or longer after you remove the trigger.
**Heat** specifically sets it off — sometimes relieved by holding cold water in the mouth.
Pain that arrives **on its own**, throbs, or wakes you at night.
It is clearly **one tooth**, often one with a deep filling, large cavity, crack, or past trauma.
Temperature pain accompanied by tenderness when biting (see [tooth pain when chewing](/blog/tooth-pain-when-chewing)).

blocks.text: This cluster — lingering, spontaneous, heat-triggered, single-tooth — is the one that commonly leads to a root canal, and it belongs on the broader list in [signs you might need a root canal](/blog/signs-you-need-a-root-canal).

sections.heading: A simple comparison

blocks.text: Use this as a guide to describe your symptoms — not as a diagnosis.

sections.heading: What to do now

blocks.text: If your sensitivity is brief and general, try a desensitising toothpaste and gentler brushing for a few weeks, and mention it at your next check-up. If it lingers, targets one tooth, or heat is a trigger, book an appointment sooner rather than later — the earlier a pulp problem is caught, the more options may remain. If you also have swelling, a bad taste, or severe or spontaneous pain, do not wait; see [dental abscess warning signs](/blog/dental-abscess-warning-signs) and consider [urgent care](/emergency-dentist-markham).

sections.heading: How a dentist sorts it out

blocks.text: Because a lingering-cold tooth and a settle-quickly tooth can look identical, your dentist will test rather than guess: comparing the suspect tooth against its neighbours with a cold test, checking the response to tapping, and taking X-rays to look for decay or changes around the root. That combination is what distinguishes reversible irritation from a pulp that needs treatment — the wider workup is described in [how dentists diagnose whether you need a root canal](/blog/how-dentists-diagnose-root-canal).

sections.heading: Everyday habits that reduce ordinary sensitivity

blocks.text: If your sensitivity fits the harmless, everyday pattern — brief, generalised, tracking with exposed roots — a few habits often help while you monitor it. (These soothe surface sensitivity; they do **not** treat a pulp problem, so they are no substitute for an exam if your symptoms fit the "pulp may be involved" list above.)

items: **Switch to a desensitising toothpaste** and use it consistently for a few weeks; the effect builds over time rather than instantly.
**Brush gently with a soft brush.** Hard scrubbing wears enamel and exposes more root surface, making sensitivity worse.
**Ease off acidic foods and drinks** — citrus, soft drinks, wine — and avoid brushing immediately after them, when enamel is temporarily softened.
**Check for clenching or grinding**, which can stress teeth and worsen sensitivity; mention it to your dentist, who may suggest a night guard.
**Don't whiten a sensitive tooth** without advice, as whitening can temporarily increase sensitivity.

blocks.text: If several weeks of these measures make no difference, or the sensitivity is clearly one tooth with a lingering or spontaneous character, that is your cue to book an assessment rather than keep experimenting at home.

sections.heading: Why "lingering" is the word that matters most

blocks.text: If you remember one thing from this article, make it the duration of the response. Everyday sensitivity is like flicking a light switch — the sensation appears with the trigger and switches off almost as fast. A pulp that is inflamed beyond recovery behaves more like a dimmer that stays lit: the pain builds and then *lingers*, sometimes for minutes, after the cold or heat is gone. That lingering quality reflects inflammation inside the tooth that keeps firing after the stimulus has passed. It is the single most useful thing you can describe to your dentist, and it is far more telling than how sharp or intense the initial jolt feels.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: My whole mouth is sensitive after whitening — is that a pulp problem?
Almost always no. Whitening commonly causes short-lived, generalised sensitivity that settles. A pulp problem is usually one tooth with lingering or spontaneous pain.
The cold sensitivity stopped suddenly. Is the tooth fine now?
Not necessarily. If a badly inflamed pulp dies, sensitivity can disappear even though the underlying problem remains. A sudden change is worth an exam.
Can sensitivity toothpaste fix a tooth that needs a root canal?
No. It can soothe everyday sensitivity, but it cannot treat an irreversibly inflamed or infected pulp.
Is heat sensitivity worse than cold sensitivity?
Heat that triggers pain — particularly when cold gives relief — is a pattern more strongly linked to an advanced pulp problem, so it is worth prompt attention.

sections.heading: Talk to us in Markham

blocks.text: If a single tooth is reacting to hot or cold and the feeling drags on, we can find out why. Explore [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham) or [arrange an exam](/appointments), and we will help you tell harmless sensitivity from a tooth that needs care.

title: Dental Abscess: Warning Signs and When to Treat It as an Emergency
seoTitle: Dental Abscess: Warning Signs and When It's an Emergency | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: A dental abscess is a pocket of infection that needs prompt care. Learn the symptoms, the red flags that mean seek help now, and how it's treated.
excerpt: A dental abscess is a pocket of infection that needs prompt care. Learn the symptoms, the red flags that mean seek help now, and how it's treated.
intro: A dental abscess is a pocket of pus caused by a bacterial infection, most often at the tip of a tooth's root or in the surrounding gum. The key thing to know up front: an abscess will not resolve permanently on its own and needs professional care — and while many are managed with a prompt appointment, certain symptoms mean you should seek help immediately. This guide helps you recognise both.

sections.heading: What an abscess actually is

blocks.text: When bacteria reach and infect the pulp inside a tooth — through deep decay, a crack, or a failed filling — the infection can travel down the root and collect in the bone at its tip. That collection is a **periapical abscess**. A related type, a **periodontal abscess**, forms in the gum tissue beside a tooth, often linked to gum disease. Both involve trapped infection under pressure, which is why they can hurt intensely and why they need to be drained and the source treated.

Treating the tooth's infected pulp is what removes the cause; that is the role of a root canal, covered in [what happens during a root canal](/blog/what-happens-during-a-root-canal). Antibiotics alone do not fix it — more on that in [antibiotics versus a root canal](/blog/antibiotics-vs-root-canal).

sections.heading: Common symptoms

blocks.text: An abscess can announce itself loudly or surprisingly quietly. Typical signs include:

items: **Throbbing, persistent pain** in a tooth or the surrounding gum, which may spread to the jaw, ear or neck on that side.
**Pain when biting or touching** the tooth.
**Swelling** of the gum, cheek or face.
**Redness and tenderness** of the gum, sometimes with a visible bump.
**A bad taste**, salty fluid, or foul smell if pus drains into the mouth.
**Sensitivity to hot and cold**, and sometimes a tooth that feels loose.
**Tender or swollen lymph nodes** under the jaw or in the neck.
**Fever** or feeling generally unwell.

blocks.text: Sometimes the pressure — and the pain — eases suddenly if the abscess bursts and drains. Relief can feel like recovery, but the infection is still there and still needs treatment.

sections.heading: Red flags: seek help immediately

blocks.text: Some symptoms suggest the infection is spreading and can become dangerous. **Treat the following as urgent:**

rows: Swelling spreading to the eye, cheek, floor of the mouth or neck
Infection tracking into deeper tissue spaces
**Medical emergency — call emergency services / go to hospital now**
Fever, chills, or feeling very unwell
Inability to fully open the mouth
Swelling affecting the muscles/spaces around the jaw

blocks.text: If you have difficulty breathing or swallowing, do not wait for a dental appointment — seek emergency medical care. For urgent dental symptoms without those life-threatening features, contact us through [emergency dental care in Markham](/emergency-dentist-markham) as soon as possible.

sections.heading: What you can do before you're seen

blocks.text: While arranging care, you can:

items: Rinse gently with warm salt water to ease discomfort and help any drainage.
Use over-the-counter pain relief **as directed on the packaging** or as advised by your pharmacist. (This article does not give doses; ask a professional about what is right for you.)
Keep your head slightly elevated when resting if throbbing worsens lying down.
Avoid very hot, cold, hard or sugary foods on that side.

blocks.text: Do **not** try to lance or squeeze the swelling yourself, and do not rely on leftover antibiotics — using antibiotics without assessment can be ineffective and contributes to resistance.

sections.heading: How a dental abscess is treated

blocks.text: Treatment has two goals: drain the infection and remove its source. Depending on the situation, that may involve:

items: **Draining the pus**, which relieves pressure and pain quickly.
**Treating the tooth** — usually a [root canal](/root-canal-markham) to remove the infected pulp and save the tooth, or, if the tooth cannot be saved, extraction.
**Antibiotics in some cases**, particularly when infection has spread or you are unwell — but as an addition to treating the tooth, not a replacement.

blocks.text: Which path fits depends on how far the infection has progressed and whether the tooth is restorable. Delaying tends to narrow the options, as we explain in [what happens if you don't get a root canal](/blog/what-happens-if-you-dont-get-a-root-canal).

sections.heading: What recovery looks like after an abscess is treated

blocks.text: Once the infection is drained and its source is treated, most people feel markedly better quickly — the relief of releasing that pressure is often dramatic. Over the following days:

items: **Pain and swelling subside** as the infection resolves. Some tenderness while the area heals is normal.
**Any prescribed medication should be finished** exactly as directed, even once you feel well, if antibiotics were given as part of treatment.
**The tooth still needs its definitive treatment completed** — draining an abscess relieves symptoms, but the tooth itself (via root canal) or its removal is what prevents the infection returning.
**Follow-up matters** — your dentist may want to check healing and, if a root canal was done, arrange the permanent restoration such as a crown.

blocks.text: If swelling or pain returns after initially improving, contact your dentist, as it can signal that the source has not been fully addressed.

sections.heading: Why an abscess should never be "waited out"

blocks.text: It is worth being blunt about this, because the temptation to wait is strong — especially when a burst abscess brings sudden relief. The relief is misleading: the infection has found a way to drain, not disappeared. Left untreated, an abscess can erode the bone around the tooth, make the tooth unsavable, and, less commonly, allow infection to spread into the deeper spaces of the face and neck, which is genuinely dangerous. Every one of those outcomes is avoidable with prompt treatment. There is no version of an abscess that gets better on its own for good, which is why "book as soon as you can" is the right instinct even on a day the pain has eased.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Will a dental abscess go away if the swelling goes down?

No. Reduced swelling or a burst abscess can bring temporary relief, but the infection remains until the tooth is treated. See [will a tooth infection go away on its own](/blog/will-a-tooth-infection-go-away).
Can I just take antibiotics and skip the dental visit?
Antibiotics may slow an infection but cannot clear one rooted in a dead or dying pulp, because they do not reach inside the tooth. The source still needs treating.
How urgent is an abscess with no swelling, just pain?
Still worth prompt care, but not necessarily an emergency. Book as soon as you can. Any spreading swelling, fever, or trouble breathing/swallowing changes that to urgent.
Does an abscess always mean I'll lose the tooth?
No. Many abscessed teeth are saved with root canal treatment once the infection is controlled, provided enough healthy tooth structure remains.

sections.heading: Get seen quickly in Markham

blocks.text: If you suspect an abscess, don't wait it out. Reach us through [emergency dental care in Markham](/emergency-dentist-markham), learn about [root canal treatment](/root-canal-markham) that removes the infection at its source, or [request an appointment](/appointments). If breathing or swallowing is affected, seek emergency medical help immediately.

title: Will a Tooth Infection Go Away on Its Own?
seoTitle: Will a Tooth Infection Go Away on Its Own? | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: Can a tooth infection heal without treatment? The honest answer, why the pain sometimes fades anyway, and what really clears an infected tooth.
primaryKeyword: will a tooth infection go away without treatment
excerpt: Can a tooth infection heal without treatment? The honest answer, why the pain sometimes fades anyway, and what really clears an infected tooth.
intro: The straightforward answer is no. Once the pulp inside a tooth becomes infected, the body cannot clear that infection by itself, because the blood supply that would normally carry immune cells and antibiotics to the area has been cut off inside the tooth. The infection can quieten, and the pain can even disappear for a while — but the source remains and tends to return, sometimes worse. This article explains *why* that is, so the reasoning makes sense rather than sounding like a scare.

sections.heading: Why a tooth is different from a cut or a cold

blocks.text: When you get a splinter or a skin infection, your immune system floods the area with blood, white cells and — if prescribed — antibiotics, and the tissue usually heals. A tooth's pulp is sealed inside hard walls of dentine and enamel with only a tiny opening at the root tip. When that pulp dies from infection, it loses its blood supply. Without circulation reaching the dead tissue inside the tooth, the body simply cannot deliver what it needs to clear the bacteria living there.

That is the core reason a tooth infection behaves differently from most infections: the battleground is inside a chamber your immune system can no longer reach. The bacteria are, in effect, protected.

sections.heading: So why does the pain sometimes stop?

blocks.text: This is where people get caught out. Pain can ease for a few reasons that do **not** mean the infection is gone:

items: **The pulp finishes dying.** A screaming nerve goes quiet once the tissue is dead. The relief is real, but the infection now sits at the root, often building toward an abscess.
**An abscess drains.** If pressure releases — through a gum bump or spontaneously — the throbbing eases while infection continues.
**Painkillers or a short antibiotic course mask it.** Symptoms recede; the cause does not.

blocks.text: A pain-free week after a bad toothache is not proof of healing. It is one of the most common reasons treatment gets postponed until an infection flares again.

sections.heading: What actually clears an infected tooth

blocks.text: Because the problem is trapped inside the tooth, the fix has to physically remove the infected tissue and seal the space. In practice that means one of two things:

items: **Root canal treatment** — removing the infected pulp, disinfecting the canals and sealing them, which lets you keep the tooth. This is the usual way to save an infected tooth; see [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham).
**Extraction** — removing the tooth entirely, which also removes the source but leaves a gap to address later.

blocks.text: Antibiotics have a role in some situations — for example, when infection has spread into surrounding tissue or you are unwell — but they are an *adjunct*, not a cure, precisely because they cannot reach dead pulp inside the tooth. We unpack that in [antibiotics versus a root canal](/blog/antibiotics-vs-root-canal).

sections.heading: The risk of waiting

blocks.text: Leaving an infected tooth is not a neutral choice. Over time it can lead to:

items: A painful **abscess** and facial **swelling** (see [dental abscess warning signs](/blog/dental-abscess-warning-signs)).
**Bone loss** around the root as the infection expands.
The tooth becoming **unrestorable**, turning a savable root canal into an extraction.
In uncommon but serious cases, infection **spreading** into deeper tissues, which can become a medical emergency.

blocks.text: The practical takeaway: acting while the tooth is still restorable usually means simpler treatment and a better chance of keeping it. The full progression is covered in [what happens if you don't get a root canal](/blog/what-happens-if-you-dont-get-a-root-canal).

sections.heading: What to do instead of waiting

items: **Book an assessment** promptly, even if the pain has eased.
**Watch for urgent signs** — spreading swelling, fever, or trouble breathing or swallowing — and treat those as emergencies.
**Manage discomfort sensibly** with over-the-counter relief used as directed and warm salt-water rinses, understanding these are holding measures, not treatment.

sections.heading: The four beliefs that keep people waiting

blocks.text: Almost everyone who delays treatment does so because of one of a handful of reasonable-sounding beliefs. It is worth naming them, because each has a catch:

items: **"It stopped hurting, so it must be healing."** More often, the pulp finished dying and simply went quiet. The infection continues at the root even though the nerve can no longer signal pain.
**"The abscess burst and drained, so it's gone."** Draining relieves pressure and pain, but the source inside the tooth remains and will refill.

**"The antibiotics cleared it."** Antibiotics can calm a spreading infection for a while, but they cannot reach and clear the dead pulp sealed inside the tooth, so the problem returns once the course ends.
**"I have no swelling, so it isn't serious."** Infection can sit quietly at the root, gradually damaging bone, long before any swelling appears.

blocks.text: Recognising your own reasoning in this list is often the nudge that turns "I'll keep an eye on it" into "I'll book the appointment."

sections.heading: What waiting actually costs

blocks.text: Because the infection persists, delay tends to move you along a predictable and unwelcome path: from a tooth that a straightforward root canal could save, toward a painful abscess, bone loss around the root, and eventually a tooth that must be extracted and replaced. Extraction plus an implant or bridge is generally more involved and more expensive than the root canal would have been — so waiting rarely saves money, and often costs more. The full progression is laid out in [what happens if you don't get a root canal](/blog/what-happens-if-you-dont-get-a-root-canal). The encouraging flip side is that acting early usually means simpler treatment and a better chance of keeping the tooth.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: My tooth stopped hurting completely. Can I cancel the dentist?
It is best not to. Pain often stops when the pulp dies, while infection continues at the root. An exam confirms what is really happening.
Can good brushing and salt-water rinses cure it?
They support your overall oral health and can ease symptoms, but they cannot reach or clear infection sealed inside a tooth.
If antibiotics helped, doesn't that mean it's treatable without a root canal?
Antibiotics can calm a spreading infection temporarily, but the tooth remains the source. Symptoms commonly return until the pulp is treated or the tooth removed.
How long can I safely wait?
There is no reliable "safe" waiting period — infections vary. The sensible approach is prompt assessment rather than watching and hoping.

sections.heading: Let's deal with the source in Markham

blocks.text: If you have (or recently had) an infected tooth, the reassuring part is that it is very treatable — the key is not to wait for it to "settle." Learn about [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham), or [request an appointment](/appointments) and we will check whether the tooth can be saved.

title: What Does a Pimple on the Gum Mean?
seoTitle: That Pimple on Your Gum: What a Gum Boil Really Means | Smile Dental Arts Centre
metaDescription: A recurring pimple or boil on the gum is often a drainage point for a tooth infection. Learn what a dental fistula is, why it comes and goes, and what to do.
excerpt: A recurring pimple or boil on the gum is often a drainage point for a tooth infection. Learn what a dental fistula is, why it comes and goes, and what to do.
intro: A small pimple, boil or bump on the gum that fills, drains a salty or bad-tasting fluid, and then seems to heal — only to come back — is most often a **sinus tract** (sometimes called a dental fistula or gum boil). It is the body's way of releasing pressure from an infection at the root of a nearby tooth. The bump itself is a symptom, not the disease, and the fact that it comes and goes is exactly why it is so easy to ignore. It should not be.

sections.heading: Why a bump forms on the gum

blocks.text: When a tooth's pulp becomes infected, pus collects at the tip of the root inside the bone. Under pressure, that infection looks for an escape route. Sometimes it tunnels through the bone and gum and opens a tiny channel on the surface — the sinus tract. Fluid drains out through this opening, which relieves the pressure and often the pain.

Because the drainage relieves pressure, the tooth may barely hurt. People frequently assume "no pain means no problem," but a draining sinus tract usually signals an ongoing infection that needs treatment. This is one of the classic quiet warning signs listed in [signs you might need a root canal](/blog/signs-you-need-a-root-canal).

sections.heading: Why it comes and goes

blocks.text: The on-off pattern trips people up. The tract can partly close, pressure builds again, the bump swells and reopens to drain, and the cycle repeats. Each "healing" is temporary. The underlying infection is still there, feeding the cycle. A bump that has appeared more than once in the same spot deserves an assessment even if it is painless right now.

sections.heading: What it usually is — and what else it could be

blocks.text: Most often, a persistent gum bump near a tooth reflects an infected or dead pulp. But not every gum lump is a sinus tract, which is another reason to have it examined rather than self-diagnose:

items: **Sinus tract from a tooth infection** — small, recurring, near a specific tooth, drains fluid. The focus of this article.
**Periodontal (gum) abscess** — infection originating in the gum pocket rather than the pulp, often with more generalised gum disease.
**Irritation or trauma** — from a sharp food, denture, or cheek/gum injury; usually settles and does not recur in the same way.
**Other soft-tissue lumps** — most are harmless, but any lump that does not resolve within about two weeks should be checked by a dentist to be safe.

blocks.text: A dentist distinguishes these with an exam and X-rays, sometimes tracing the tract to its source tooth.

sections.heading: How the source is found and treated

blocks.text: Finding which tooth is responsible is important, because the bump may not sit directly over the culprit. Your dentist may:

items: **Take X-rays**, occasionally placing a small flexible point into the tract so the image shows where it leads.
**Test nearby teeth** for their response to cold or tapping to identify the non-vital tooth.

blocks.text: Once the source is confirmed, treatment addresses the infection itself:

items: **Root canal treatment** to remove the infected pulp, which usually allows the sinus tract to heal and close on its own. See [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham).
**Extraction**, if the tooth cannot be saved.
If the bump is a gum-related abscess rather than a pulp problem, treatment targets the gum infection instead.

blocks.text: Antibiotics are not a stand-alone solution here, because they do not clear infection sealed inside a tooth — the same principle explained in [will a tooth infection go away on its own](/blog/will-a-tooth-infection-go-away).

sections.heading: What to do now

items: **Don't pop or squeeze it.** Let it be; squeezing can push infection into surrounding tissue.
**Rinse gently** with warm salt water for comfort.
**Book an assessment** even if it is painless and even if it has drained and "healed."

**Book a prompt routine appointment** for a simple recurring bump. If it ever escalates to spreading facial swelling, fever, or difficulty breathing or swallowing, treat that as urgent — see [dental abscess warning signs](/blog/dental-abscess-warning-signs) and [urgent care in Markham](/emergency-dentist-markham).

sections.heading: What the drainage and the taste are telling you

blocks.text: The salty or unpleasant fluid that comes from a gum bump is pus — the product of your body walling off and trying to discharge an infection. That your body has created a drainage channel is, in a grim way, a sign of a chronic (long-standing) rather than acute situation: the infection has been present long enough to establish a route out. This is why a sinus tract is often relatively painless. Pressure, which is what causes most dental pain, keeps escaping instead of building. So the very feature that makes the bump easy to ignore — the lack of pain — is also a clue that the infection has been quietly persisting.

sections.heading: Why treating it early protects more than the tooth

blocks.text: Addressing a draining sinus tract promptly is not only about the tooth itself. An ongoing infection at the root gradually affects the surrounding bone, and the longer it continues, the more bone can be lost around the root tip. Treating the source early — usually with a root canal that lets the tract heal and close — tends to mean:

items: **A better chance of saving the tooth**, before decay or infection make it unrestorable.
**Less bone involvement** to contend with.
**Fewer surprises**, since a chronic tract can flare into a painful, swollen abscess without much warning.

blocks.text: In other words, the painless bump is an opportunity: it is the infection showing itself while things are still relatively simple to treat. Acting on it is far easier than waiting for the flare-up that often eventually comes.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: It doesn't hurt at all — do I really need to see a dentist?
Yes. A painless, draining bump is a common sign of a chronic infection. The lack of pain reflects the pressure escaping, not the problem resolving.
Will the bump go away if I just keep it clean?
Good hygiene helps your mouth overall, but it will not clear infection inside a tooth. The bump typically closes for good only once the source is treated.
Can it turn into something serious?
A chronic tract can flare into a painful, swollen abscess, and ongoing infection can damage the bone around the root. Prompt treatment avoids that.
How long should I wait to see if it clears up?
Any gum lump that lasts beyond about two weeks, or that keeps returning to the same spot, should be examined.

sections.heading: Have it checked in Markham

blocks.text: If a bump on your gum keeps coming back, we can trace it to its source and treat the cause — not just the symptom. Read about [root canal treatment in Markham](/root-canal-markham) or [book an exam](/appointments).
